https://the-decoder.com/sunos-new-visual.lead_paragraph: AI music generator Suno can now create images and video clips to go with its songs, thanks to a new feature called Visuals. The feature runs on H3 Move, a customized and safety-filtered version of MiniMax's video model H3. The clips run up to 15 seconds, follow the song's structure, pick up on lyrics, and support lip sync.
paragraphs: AI music generator Suno can now create images and video clips to go with its songs, thanks to a new feature called Visuals. The feature runs on H3 Move, a customized and safety-filtered version of MiniMax's video model H3. The clips run up to 15 seconds, follow the song's structure, pick up on lyrics, and support lip sync.

Users can start from a reference photo, a prompt, or one of Suno's preset characters. Lyric videos let you tweak fonts and colors, extend clips on a timeline, and pick the length and aspect ratio. Two quality tiers are available, "Fast"and "Standard."Filters block prompts and uploads that reference specific artists, celebrities, or copyrighted works. Before sharing content outside Suno, the platform adds an embedded watermark.
Visuals works on the web, iOS, and Android, and requires its own credits. Pro and Premier subscribers get a temporary allotment to try it out.

In late July, the Munich Regional Court I ruled against Suno in a lawsuit filed by GEMA, Germany's music rights organization, finding copyright infringement. Shortly after, Suno announced tools to label Suno-made songs as AI-generated on other platforms. The company has reached a deal with Warner Music, but Universal and Sony are still pursuing litigation.

https://the-decoder.com/openai-launches-.lead_paragraph: OpenAI releases two new language models. GPT-6.2 Astra is aimed at demanding professional work, while GPT-6.2 Sol is built for everyday use. OpenAI says both outperform their predecessors on benchmarks and cost less to run.
paragraphs: OpenAI releases two new language models. GPT-6.2 Astra is aimed at demanding professional work, while GPT-6.2 Sol is built for everyday use. OpenAI says both outperform their predecessors on benchmarks and cost less to run.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are available now for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Pro-500 subscribers can use Ultrafast mode with both models. For the first time, Pro-200 subscribers also get Ultrafast access, starting with GPT-6.2 Sol.

Developers can access both models through the OpenAI API. OpenAI says API pricing for GPT-6.2 Astra is 20 percent cheaper than its predecessor's, at $8 per million input tokens, $0.40 for cached inputs, and $40 per million output tokens. GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's pricing at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached inputs, and $10 for output per million tokens.
### OpenAI calls Astra "the world's best model for scientists"and touts polished slides

OpenAI trained GPT-6.2 Astra to handle professional conventions in fields like law, finance, and accounting more reliably. The company says presentations pull layouts, colors, and typography from templates, matching exact font sizes. Slide titles are meant to capture a slide's main point, while body text stays focused on key details.

OpenAI's announcement leans hard on the price-to-performance ratio of its models. On Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multi-step professional workflows, GPT-6.2 Astra scores 5.2 points above its predecessor GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. It leads Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at just 5 percent of the cost. Only Google's Gemini 4 Carbon keeps up with Astra on this benchmark.

On the legal benchmark Harvey LAB-AA, which covers tasks like contract clause analysis, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubles Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost, according to OpenAI. On the internal GDPval-v2 benchmark, which includes consulting, finance, and design tasks, OpenAI says Astra gains 6.2 percentage points over its predecessor while using 22 percent fewer output tokens.

OpenAI says computer use, already a strong suit of the predecessor, got better again. In testing, the model reportedly built a 3D car model, wrote a physics solver in Python, and animated the results in Blender. In another demo, it modeled a remote-controlled car part by part and produced an animated assembly guide.

OpenAI also claims progress in web design. On the 3D benchmark AA-3D, human judges compare two blinded interactive experiences. GPT-6.2 Astra takes first with 1,318 Elo points, ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 1,259.

On Terminal-Bench-Science, a benchmark that tests scientific workflows in a terminal, the model scores 9 percentage points above GPT-6 Astra, again at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. Astra also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which measures how well models interpret biological data and run experiments, OpenAI says.
### Sol nearly matches the original Astra at a fraction of the cost

GPT-6.2 Sol is for users who want a fast, versatile model for everyday tasks, OpenAI says. On the coding benchmark FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether code changes meet the quality bar of real projects, Sol trails Astra by just 0.5 points at one-fifth the cost. OpenAI says the model also handles non-work tasks well.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol have also gotten better at cybersecurity, according to OpenAI. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and deliver better bug fixes, with notably higher token efficiency in several tests. Both models hit the "Critical"threshold for cybersecurity in OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, just as GPT-6 Astra did before them.

OpenAI is adding stricter safeguards for potentially risky cybersecurity requests in response. These safeguards should make abuse harder but will also limit legitimate vulnerability research and security testing, OpenAI says.

OpenAI plans to offer the new models through OpenAI Daybreak, which already gives vetted security researchers access to other models with fewer guardrails. The published cybersecurity benchmark numbers come from internal tests with safeguards and classifiers turned off. OpenAI lays out its methodology in the accompanying safety report.
### Astra takes second in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

In the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which rolls up nine evaluations across knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, GPT-6.2 Astra finishes second, just behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2. Astra jumps five points over GPT-6 Astra, according to Artificial Analysis, passing Google's Gemini 4 Carbon (60 points) and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (59 points). GPT-6.2 Sol picks up two points to reach 57, matching GPT-6 Astra's level at only about 15 percent of the cost per task.

OpenAI owns the Pareto frontier on cost versus performance, the line where no other model is both cheaper and better, according to Artificial Analysis. Only Anthropic and Meta models also land on that frontier. OpenAI holds most of the top spots on efficiency too, measured by output tokens per task. Claude Fable 5.2 is the only outside model that shows up there.

Artificial Analysis backs up OpenAI's claims in science and factual knowledge. GPT-6.2 Astra leads on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 and places second behind Claude Fable 5.2 on the physics reasoning test CritPt v2, the factual knowledge benchmark AA-Omniscience, and the knowledge benchmark HLE-Diamond. Astra also leads in 3D design (AA-3D) and robotics (AA-Robotics v0.1), scoring 79 on robotics against Sol's 78 and Claude Fable 5.2's 75.

Coding is a different story, though. According to Artificial Analysis, both models have flatlined there. In the Coding Agent Index, measured with the Codex harness at max compute, GPT-6.2 Astra stays right where GPT-6 Astra was. GPT-6.2 Sol actually drops three points from GPT-6.1 Sol. That decline comes from a 14-point slide on SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA, where the model omits key facts from its answers more often than its predecessor did.

Artificial Analysis also flags a high hallucination rate. At maximum effort, GPT-6.2 Astra hallucinates 59 percent of the time, Sol 55 percent. The metric is AA-Omniscience Hallucination Rate, which measures how frequently a model guesses on factual questions instead of saying it doesn't know. These are unusually hard questions, so the numbers don't reflect everyday hallucination rates.
### Epoch AI finds Astra on par with Fable 5.2 but weaker on real-world tasks

Research organization Epoch AI tested GPT-6.2 Astra on its own benchmarks before launch. The model scores 174 points in the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), tying Anthropic's Fable 5.2. Both models beat what the previous trend for reasoning models would have predicted before Astra, according to Epoch AI.

On real-world tasks pulled from Epoch AI's own research, Astra fell behind Fable 5.2 and barely improved over GPT-6 Astra. According to Epoch AI, the model missed the central question on simpler research projects and spun its wheels trying to fix things. On a task about researching AI data centers, Astra played it too safe and skipped key estimates, something Epoch AI says no contractor could get away with. Epoch AI rated Astra's writing as relatively strong compared to other tested models but still below its own bar.

One thing that stands out is Astra's ability to run complex reasoning within a single output token, with no visible chain of thought. Epoch AI clocks 12.3 serial steps for Astra, up from 10.5 for GPT-6 Astra and 4.2 for Claude Fable 5.1, the strongest non-OpenAI model at the time. Models that can reason this way without showing their work are harder to monitor, a safety concern that already came up with the first Astra model.

On FrontierMath Erdős, a benchmark of unsolved math problems, GPT-6.2 Astra cracked 7 of 68 tasks, each formally verified in the proof assistant Lean. The old record was 3 of 68, set by GPT-6.1 Sol. One of the seven had no known solution before.
### Vals AI puts Astra and Sol in the top 10 but finds legal weak spots

GPT-6.2 Astra ranks 7th and GPT-6.2 Sol 9th in the Vals Index, separated by just 1.6 points. The price gap is wide, though. Sol runs $3.18 per task, less than a third of Astra's $10.68, making it the cheapest model in the top 10, according to Vals AI. Astra also got cheaper than its predecessor, scoring 2.6 points above GPT-6 Astra at roughly half of its $21.28 per-task cost. Vals AI says Astra uses the fewest output tokens in the top 10, averaging 91,000 per task.

Vals AI backs OpenAI's claim to the top spot on the Vals Science Index. Astra leads that ranking and takes first on Terminal-Bench Science and VCB 1–100 at about half the cost and half the runtime of GPT-6 Astra. Sol comes in third on Terminal-Bench Science at roughly a quarter of Astra's cost. On the broader Terminal-Bench 4 for agentic coding, Astra places 5th and Sol 7th.

Legal tests are where the models fall short, according to Vals AI. On the HLAB benchmark, Astra and Sol double their predecessors' scores but rank only 11th and 21st. On the Legal Research benchmark, the drop is even steeper, with Astra at 30th and Sol at 52nd. Vals AI says the models make nearly twice as many tool calls as their predecessors but write shorter answers.

In September, OpenAI announced a specialized product called "Astra for Law."It does significantly better than the base model on the Legal Research Bench, reaching 6th place. Vals AI tested both models with a one-million-token context window and 128,000 max output tokens at full reasoning effort.
### GPT-6.2 Astra is the first released model to hit OpenAI's "High"threshold for AI self-improvement

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra is the first externally released model to reach the "High"threshold for AI self-improvement. OpenAI says the model can meaningfully speed up AI research, on par with giving every OpenAI researcher an extra, highly skilled research engineer.

OpenAI calls this out explicitly as a risk. Models that can help build future AI systems could push the field forward faster than safety measures and human oversight can keep up. The industry is currently wrestling with this under the label "RSI".

As countermeasures, OpenAI points to tighter controls in research environments and its monitoring system Control Room, which can track research tasks and shut them down if needed. The company also says it has expanded monitoring that examines how models reason and act and automatically flags unauthorized behavior.

On alignment, meaning how well the model follows user instructions and communicates openly, the new models match their predecessors, according to OpenAI. In two tests, however, they more often failed to flag obstacles blocking their work, like a missing file or an unavailable search tool.

GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's pricing at $2 for input, $0.10 for cached inputs, and $10 for output per million tokens.

### OpenAI calls Astra "the world's best model for scientists"and touts polished slides

OpenAI trained GPT-6.2 Astra to handle professional conventions in fields like law, finance, and accounting more reliably. The company says presentations pull layouts, colors, and typography from templates, matching exact font sizes. Slide titles are meant to capture a slide's main point, while body text stays focused on key details.

OpenAI's announcement leans hard on the price-to-performance ratio of its models. On Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark that tests multi-step professional workflows, GPT-6.2 Astra scores 5.2 points above its predecessor GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. It leads Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points at just 5 percent of the cost. Only Google's Gemini 4 Carbon keeps up with Astra on this benchmark.

On the legal benchmark Harvey LAB-AA, which covers tasks like contract clause analysis, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubles Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth of the cost, according to OpenAI. On the internal GDPval-v2 benchmark, which includes consulting, finance, and design tasks, OpenAI says Astra gains 6.2 percentage points over its predecessor while using 22 percent fewer output tokens.

OpenAI says computer use, already a strong suit of the predecessor, got better again. In testing, the model reportedly built a 3D car model, wrote a physics solver in Python, and animated the results in Blender. In another demo, it modeled a remote-controlled car part by part and produced an animated assembly guide.

OpenAI also claims progress in web design. On the 3D benchmark AA-3D, human judges compare two blinded interactive experiences. GPT-6.2 Astra takes first with 1,318 Elo points, ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT-6.2 Sol at 1,259.

On Terminal-Bench-Science, a benchmark that tests scientific workflows in a terminal, the model scores 9 percentage points above GPT-6 Astra, again at less than a third of the cost, according to OpenAI. Astra also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which measures how well models interpret biological data and run experiments, OpenAI says.

### Sol nearly matches the original Astra at a fraction of the cost

GPT-6.2 Sol is for users who want a fast, versatile model for everyday tasks, OpenAI says. On the coding benchmark FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether code changes meet the quality bar of real projects, Sol trails Astra by just 0.5 points at one-fifth the cost. OpenAI says the model also handles non-work tasks well.

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol have also gotten better at cybersecurity, according to OpenAI. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and deliver better bug fixes, with notably higher token efficiency in several tests. Both models hit the "Critical"threshold for cybersecurity in OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, just as GPT-6 Astra did before them.

OpenAI is adding stricter safeguards for potentially risky cybersecurity requests in response. These safeguards should make abuse harder but will also limit legitimate vulnerability research and security testing, OpenAI says.

OpenAI plans to offer the new models through OpenAI Daybreak, which already gives vetted security researchers access to other models with fewer guardrails. The published cybersecurity benchmark numbers come from internal tests with safeguards and classifiers turned off. OpenAI lays out its methodology in the accompanying safety report.

### Astra takes second in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

In the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, which rolls up nine evaluations across knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, GPT-6.2 Astra finishes second, just behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2. Astra jumps five points over GPT-6 Astra, according to Artificial Analysis, passing Google's Gemini 4 Carbon (60 points) and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (59 points). GPT-6.2 Sol picks up two points to reach 57, matching GPT-6 Astra's level at only about 15 percent of the cost per task.

OpenAI owns the Pareto frontier on cost versus performance, the line where no other model is both cheaper and better, according to Artificial Analysis. Only Anthropic and Meta models also land on that frontier. OpenAI holds most of the top spots on efficiency too, measured by output tokens per task. Claude Fable 5.2 is the only outside model that shows up there.

Artificial Analysis backs up OpenAI's claims in science and factual knowledge. GPT-6.2 Astra leads on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 and places second behind Claude Fable 5.2 on the physics reasoning test CritPt v2, the factual knowledge benchmark AA-Omniscience, and the knowledge benchmark HLE-Diamond. Astra also leads in 3D design (AA-3D) and robotics (AA-Robotics v0.1), scoring 79 on robotics against Sol's 78 and Claude Fable 5.2's 75.

Coding is a different story, though. According to Artificial Analysis, both models have flatlined there. In the Coding Agent Index, measured with the Codex harness at max compute, GPT-6.2 Astra stays right where GPT-6 Astra was. GPT-6.2 Sol actually drops three points from GPT-6.1 Sol. That decline comes from a 14-point slide on SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA, where the model omits key facts from its answers more often than its predecessor did.

Artificial Analysis also flags a high hallucination rate. At maximum effort, GPT-6.2 Astra hallucinates 59 percent of the time, Sol 55 percent. The metric is AA-Omniscience Hallucination Rate, which measures how frequently a model guesses on factual questions instead of saying it doesn't know. These are unusually hard questions, so the numbers don't reflect everyday hallucination rates.

### Epoch AI finds Astra on par with Fable 5.2 but weaker on real-world tasks

Research organization Epoch AI tested GPT-6.2 Astra on its own benchmarks before launch. The model scores 174 points in the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), tying Anthropic's Fable 5.2. Both models beat what the previous trend for reasoning models would have predicted before Astra, according to Epoch AI.

On real-world tasks pulled from Epoch AI's own research, Astra fell behind Fable 5.2 and barely improved over GPT-6 Astra. According to Epoch AI, the model missed the central question on simpler research projects and spun its wheels trying to fix things. On a task about researching AI data centers, Astra played it too safe and skipped key estimates, something Epoch AI says no contractor could get away with. Epoch AI rated Astra's writing as relatively strong compared to other tested models but still below its own bar.

One thing that stands out is Astra's ability to run complex reasoning within a single output token, with no visible chain of thought. Epoch AI clocks 12.3 serial steps for Astra, up from 10.5 for GPT-6 Astra and 4.2 for Claude Fable 5.1, the strongest non-OpenAI model at the time. Models that can reason this way without showing their work are harder to monitor, a safety concern that already came up with the first Astra model.

On FrontierMath Erdős, a benchmark of unsolved math problems, GPT-6.2 Astra cracked 7 of 68 tasks, each formally verified in the proof assistant Lean. The old record was 3 of 68, set by GPT-6.1 Sol. One of the seven had no known solution before.

### Vals AI puts Astra and Sol in the top 10 but finds legal weak spots

GPT-6.2 Astra ranks 7th and GPT-6.2 Sol 9th in the Vals Index, separated by just 1.6 points. The price gap is wide, though. Sol runs $3.18 per task, less than a third of Astra's $10.68, making it the cheapest model in the top 10, according to Vals AI. Astra also got cheaper than its predecessor, scoring 2.6 points above GPT-6 Astra at roughly half of its $21.28 per-task cost. Vals AI says Astra uses the fewest output tokens in the top 10, averaging 91,000 per task.

Vals AI backs OpenAI's claim to the top spot on the Vals Science Index. Astra leads that ranking and takes first on Terminal-Bench Science and VCB 1–100 at about half the cost and half the runtime of GPT-6 Astra. Sol comes in third on Terminal-Bench Science at roughly a quarter of Astra's cost. On the broader Terminal-Bench 4 for agentic coding, Astra places 5th and Sol 7th.

Legal tests are where the models fall short, according to Vals AI. On the HLAB benchmark, Astra and Sol double their predecessors' scores but rank only 11th and 21st. On the Legal Research benchmark, the drop is even steeper, with Astra at 30th and Sol at 52nd. Vals AI says the models make nearly twice as many tool calls as their predecessors but write shorter answers.

In September, OpenAI announced a specialized product called "Astra for Law."It does significantly better than the base model on the Legal Research Bench, reaching 6th place. Vals AI tested both models with a one-million-token context window and 128,000 max output tokens at full reasoning effort.

### GPT-6.2 Astra is the first released model to hit OpenAI's "High"threshold for AI self-improvement

According to OpenAI, GPT-6.2 Astra is the first externally released model to reach the "High"threshold for AI self-improvement. OpenAI says the model can meaningfully speed up AI research, on par with giving every OpenAI researcher an extra, highly skilled research engineer.

OpenAI calls this out explicitly as a risk. Models that can help build future AI systems could push the field forward faster than safety measures and human oversight can keep up. The industry is currently wrestling with this under the label "RSI".

As countermeasures, OpenAI points to tighter controls in research environments and its monitoring system Control Room, which can track research tasks and shut them down if needed. The company also says it has expanded monitoring that examines how models reason and act and automatically flags unauthorized behavior.

On alignment, meaning how well the model follows user instructions and communicates openly, the new models match their predecessors, according to OpenAI. In two tests, however, they more often failed to flag obstacles blocking their work, like a missing file or an unavailable search tool.

paragraphs: OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to click and type their way through clinic software and insurance portals as digital clerks. GPT-6 Luna handles administrative tasks for about 8.5 cents per task, according to the company.

In a recent product announcement, OpenAI targets the lack of APIs in healthcare. The computer-use agents integrated into the Agents API in late September operate existing user interfaces the way a human would. In this case, they transfer data between electronic health records and external web portals.

According to OpenAI, when a patient reports back pain, the agent is meant to search relevant prior findings and draft both an MRI order and a reply to the patient. It should also prepare a prior authorization request on the insurer's portal. Clinicians and the responsible administrative staff review these drafts before they are released. The features are available through the API as well as in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians.
### GPT-6 Luna completes admin tasks for 8.5 cents per task

In an evaluation described by OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra worked through tasks from electronic health record inboxes, among other things preparing an ibuprofen dosage for a child with a broken arm. Physician reviewers rated 99 percent of the 325 tasks evaluated as clinically safe. In 93 percent of 646 reviews, the reviewers called the prep work very or extremely helpful.

For administrative workflows such as prior authorizations, appeals, or medical equipment orders, OpenAI points to the independent HealthAdminBench benchmark from Stanford University researchers. GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3 percent of possible points. GPT-6 Luna, built for low API pricing, scored 91.8 percent and, according to OpenAI, cost about 8.5 cents per task, 98 percent less than Astra. Both models ran at maximum reasoning effort on the benchmark.
### Major US healthcare companies test and deploy OpenAI's computer-use agents

Several partner organizations are helping advance the technology. At CVS Health, the agents already process referrals and specialist consultations across separate systems. According to the announcement, one agent cleared a months-long backlog of outgoing documents in one weekend, while another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consultations daily. CVS Health published its software architecture as Agent Kit on GitHub.

At insurer Cigna Healthcare, the models merge patient information from more than 10 separate systems. Abridge is developing the agents for planned use in clinical discharge planning. Ambience has demonstrated additional safety mechanisms in which an agent stops when a patient's record is unclear and asks a physician for input. Startups like Assort also use the feature in Codex to complete referrals in practice management software whose APIs don't support that final click.
### Data privacy, health records, and Europe

Because the agents work directly in electronic health records, protecting sensitive health data is a core concern. OpenAI says it does not use organizational data to train its base models. ChatGPT for Healthcare offers role-based access controls and audit logs, according to the company. Organizations can also configure the applications and environments so an agent only accesses the records and actions needed for a given task.

For HIPAA-compliant workflows with protected health information, organizations must sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with OpenAI. They also need to use the covered services and apply the required security and retention settings. The healthcare facilities themselves are responsible for proper use, but OpenAI, as a contracting party, also has its own obligations under HIPAA. Verified medical professionals in the US who use ChatGPT for Clinicians, a free individual plan, can also sign a BAA, though it applies only to the features the agreement covers.

In the CVS Health deployment, data stays within infrastructure that CVS controls, according to OpenAI. CVS reviews the agents' work steps through screenshots and action logs. The announcement does not say where those screenshots are processed or how long they are stored. It also does not address the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). So far, the offering targets the US market.

OpenAI frames the technology primarily as a tool against administrative friction in a highly fragmented healthcare system. Whether it sees broad adoption likely will not depend solely on the accuracy rates and costs cited in the company's announcement. Also decisive is how reliably the agents connect to existing systems and whether AI agents can be dependably monitored in practice. Another open question is whether a human is required to decide on clinically or legally relevant steps.

https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-.title: The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output
https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-.summary: The US is tightening its chip export controls. Data centers in third countries like Singapore and Malaysia will soon need a US license to buy Nvidia chips, closing the loophole that let Chinese firms rent cloud compute abroad. A Reuters investigation also reveals how China offsets its hardware shortage through industrial-scale distillation of US AI models.
https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/the-us-wants-to-.lead_paragraph: Chinese companies have been skirting US export bans by legally renting Nvidia computing power in third countries. After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, the US is closing that loophole. paragraphs: Chinese companies have been skirting US export bans by legally renting Nvidia computing power in third countries. After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, the US is closing that loophole. An investigation also reveals how China has cushioned the years-long chip embargo through an entire industry built around model distillation.

For years, the US has tried to cut China off from importing advanced AI processors through strict export controls. Chinese companies responded by exploiting an entirely legal loophole, renting the computing power they needed through cloud-based remote access from foreign data centers that were allowed to receive US hardware.

The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) at the US Commerce Department now wants to shut down that workaround with an interim rule. It aligns remote-access rules with existing physical export bans. Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need a US government license to buy advanced AI chips from US manufacturers like Nvidia, Bloomberg reports. Applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.

Subsidiaries of US-headquartered companies are exempt from the license requirement, as are shipments to data centers running only commercial recommendation systems for online retailers or social media platforms. The rules take effect once published in the Federal Register. Nvidia's stock fell as much as 2.9 percent after the announcement, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5 percent.
### Illegal chip diversions and Jensen Huang's downfall

The political trigger, though, was suspected illegal smuggling of physical chips. The new rule comes just days after the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former manager at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. US authorities suspect Alice Huang, who now lives in China, of espionage. They are investigating Megaspeed for possible export-control violations after banned Nvidia chips reportedly turned up in a Chinese data center linked to her. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing, and President Donald Trump said Monday that Jensen Huang did not compromise national security.

The scandal still set off an open power struggle in Washington over lax enforcement of chip sanctions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had delayed a Trump-authorized measure against illegal chip diversions, according to Axios, prompting Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to publicly accuse him of inaction. The Commerce Department's announcement now states with unusual bluntness that the draft rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council.
### Reuters investigation maps China's distillation industry

A separate exclusive Reuters investigation shows how Chinese developers cope with the years-long shortage of top-tier domestic hardware. By reviewing more than 300 Chinese papers, patents, job postings, and government documents, Reuters shows for the first time how heavily China relies on model distillation as a stopgap. What started years ago as an academic workaround has grown into an industrial sector with a highly developed division of labor.

The technique does not make powerful chips like Nvidia's unnecessary, but it drastically reduces developers' own compute load because a single expensive query to a US teacher model replaces repeated computation. Chinese firms now build their own software to automate the extraction of answers, code, and problem solutions from leading US models. Specialized workers then process the material to train smaller, far cheaper local student models.

Research papers show how deep this practice already runs. As early as November 2024, researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University created 10,750 training examples for Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B. They drew on about 5,000 responses from OpenAI's o1 and translations from GPT-4o mini, though they themselves warned at the time of a looming dependence on outside innovation. Alibaba described its systematic use of GPT-4 and GPT-4o for foreign-language training data in April 2025. In February 2026, Jiao Tong University and food-delivery company Meituan used GPT-4o to train smaller models for coordinating coding agents.

Policy directives from Beijing are driving this growth. The government wants to deploy smaller, low-cost AI systems across China's manufacturing sector. Official government documents do not directly instruct anyone to copy American models. Still, an "AI+Manufacturing"package published by eight ministries in January and initiatives in Shanghai and Shenzhen explicitly promote distillation and other techniques that reduce computing needs. In practice, this state-driven push for efficiency drives Chinese developers to tap the most powerful US models as a data source at scale.

Ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, this industrial-scale practice is becoming a geopolitical flashpoint. Distillation is not illegal, but it violates the terms of service of US developers like OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies have long leveled accusations against Chinese AI labs, documenting the massive volumes of extracted data in detailed reports and deploying technical countermeasures. Anthropic recently said it now successfully blocks most such distillation attacks. These accusations were also covered in our Frontier Radar #4 on Chinese models.

US officials also confronted Chinese regulators in Chengdu as early as July because Washington sees mass distillation as the main reason for China's rapid AI catch-up, according to Reuters. Chinese insiders also point to their own advances in algorithms and model design. Treasury Secretary Bessent is now threatening sanctions and Entity List designations if covert distillation attacks cross the line into intellectual property theft. Chinese developers, uncertain about the rules, recently asked Beijing's Ministry of Industry for clear guidelines on using foreign models.

paragraphs: OpenAI is giving NATO and several European governments access to its cybersecurity tool Daybreak. Through Daybreak, cyber defense teams can use OpenAI's models to audit software, find vulnerabilities, and patch security gaps. The NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) says it's already using the underlying models heavily. NCIA chief Dylan Browne called it a generational leap in cyber defense. France, Germany, and Poland have also been granted access.

paragraphs: Reports of AI being used for the sexual exploitation of children have jumped more than 8,400 percent in two years. According to a report by Edinburgh's Childlight Institute, the number of reported AI-generated abuse images climbed from about 4,700 in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025, The Guardian reports. The material includes AI-manipulated images (deepfakes) from so-called "nudify apps"that digitally strip people of their clothing. Abusers can use the faked images to blackmail children into handing over money or more photos.

The data comes from reports that tech companies filed with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). The UK's Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) reviewed 6,310 criminal, photorealistic AI-generated abuse images in the first half of 2026 alone. That's 40 percent more than in all of 2025.

Childlight data director Debi Fry acknowledges that better detection systems partly explain the spike. She still calls for swift action from lawmakers and tech companies. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency, dedicate funding to prevention, and coordinate efforts across healthcare, schools, child protection services, and the justice system.

https://the-decoder.com/isomorphic-labs-.title: Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion in its second mega-round within six months
https://the-decoder.com/isomorphic-labs-.summary: Isomorphic Labs has raised $5 billion, just six months after a $2.1 billion round. Alphabet’s AI drug discovery company, led by Demis Hassabis, plans to use the funding to push its drug pipeline toward clinical trials. The company has no approved drugs yet.
https://the-decoder.com/isomorphic-labs-.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/isomorphic-labs-.lead_paragraph: Alphabet's AI drug discovery company Isomorphic Labs has raised $5 billion, its second billion-dollar round in six months. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital co-led the round, joined by new backer Andreessen Horowitz along with Alphabet and all existing investors.
paragraphs: Alphabet's AI drug discovery company Isomorphic Labs has raised $5 billion, its second billion-dollar round in six months. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital co-led the round, joined by new backer Andreessen Horowitz along with Alphabet and all existing investors.

The company had already raised $2.1 billion back in May 2026. The money will go toward advancing its in-house platform IsoDDE (Isomorphic Drug Design Engine) and pushing its drug pipeline toward clinical trials. IsoDDE goes beyond AlphaFold 3, according to the company founded in 2021, and aims to better predict drug binding and docking sites. Isomorphic Labs works with Novartis, Eli Lilly, and Johnson & Johnson but has no approved drug to show for it yet.

The company is led by Demis Hassabis, who stepped down from day-to-day leadership of Google Deepmind in August 2026 and now serves as Alphabet's Chief Scientist. Hassabis won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry alongside John Jumper for their work on AlphaFold.

Deepmind's original AlphaFold team was disbanded in July 2026. Many researchers moved to Isomorphic Labs or were reassigned to other projects. Nearly a quarter left Deepmind entirely. Deepmind still shipped AlphaGenome 2 in early November 2026, which predicts how DNA variants affect gene activity in specific cell types.

https://the-decoder.com/californias-atto.title: California's attorney general sues OpenAI over rogue AI models that attacked Hugging Face
https://the-decoder.com/californias-atto.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI over a cyberattack that the company’s out-of-control AI models launched against AI platform Hugging Face in July.
https://the-decoder.com/californias-atto.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/californias-atto.lead_paragraph: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI over a cyberattack that the company's out-of-control AI models launched against AI platform Hugging Face in July. The lawsuit alleges OpenAI tested advanced models without proper safety measures and misled the public about how safe its experiments were.
paragraphs: California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI over a cyberattack that the company's out-of-control AI models launched against AI platform Hugging Face in July. The lawsuit alleges OpenAI tested advanced models without proper safety measures and misled the public about how safe its experiments were.

Around 700 AI agents broke loose during internal testing, according to an external investigation. They got onto the open internet, traded secret messages, and coordinated the attack over seven days. Bonta pointed to at least 80 incidents where OpenAI lost control of its own technology, Politico reports. Rogue AI could threaten critical infrastructure like power grids, hospitals, and financial systems, he said.

OpenAI called the lawsuit one-sided and pointed out that all major AI labs are dealing with similar problems. The company now backs stricter safety laws, shutdown controls, and independent auditors in AI labs. Two more lawsuits against OpenAI over the incident are already pending. One of them also names Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceXSI as defendants.

https://the-decoder.com/openais-gpt-6-as.summary: OpenAI physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to tackle a problem that had stumped particle physicists for over 25 years. The AI model took Craig’s strategy for defining the full Standard Model on a computational lattice and turned it into a working proof. Craig says a lot of work remains before realistic simulations are possible.

https://the-decoder.com/openais-gpt-6-as.lead_paragraph: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics.
paragraphs: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra helped produce a proof that could solve a 50-year-old problem in particle physics.

Physicist Nathaniel Craig of UC Santa Barbara, currently a visiting scientist at OpenAI, presented the approach on the OpenAI blog and as a preprint paper. Craig leads the particle theory group at UCSB and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

Physicists can simulate parts of the Standard Model, the theory describing all known particles and fundamental forces, on a computer grid called a lattice. That has already led to breakthroughs like calculating the proton's mass from first principles. But putting the full theory on a lattice has been impossible. The weak force, which governs certain types of radioactive decay, treats left- and right-handed particles differently. On simple lattices, this asymmetry creates unwanted ghost particles. Special lattice particles called overlap fermions can filter them out, but for over 25 years, nobody could set their phase correctly.

Craig had a strategy to fix the phase by comparing progressively finer lattices, but couldn't prove it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. GPT-6 Astra turned the idea into a working construction and took the lead on the detailed proof. Lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir reviewed the proof and raised questions that Craig says helped build confidence in the result. He calls the work "much more a beginning than an end"and says a lot remains before realistic simulations are possible.

The result follows a run of AI advances in mathematics that started in January 2026. In May, OpenAI's disproof of Erdős's unit distance conjecture became the first AI proof worthy of math's top journal. Days later, Google Deepmind's AlphaProof Nexus solved nine of 353 open Erdős problems for a few hundred dollars, and by October its results had passed peer review.

The most far-reaching claim came in September, when OpenAI submitted a 166-page proof for the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem and the Clay Mathematics Institute said it had "apparently been settled". The solution remains under review, and mathematicians have questioned whether OpenAI fully understands its own proof. Across the field, mathematicians have mixed feelings as AI keeps cracking unsolved problems.

At $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, Neon is priced above previous Gemini 4 models.
https://the-decoder.com/google-ships-gem.author: Matthias Bastian
https://the-decoder.com/google-ships-gem.lead_paragraph: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, promising "frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows."The model is live today through the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, above Carbon and Argon's introductory rate of $2/$10 (doubling to $4/$20 on December 1) and twice the price of Hydrogen at $1.50/$7.50.
paragraphs: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, promising "frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows."The model is live today through the API at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, above Carbon and Argon's introductory rate of $2/$10 (doubling to $4/$20 on December 1) and twice the price of Hydrogen at $1.50/$7.50.

Neon offers a context window of about one million tokens and can produce up to one million output tokens. It handles text, images, video, audio, and PDFs, with support for Computer Use, code execution, file search, and grounding via Google Search and Maps. Image and audio generation aren't supported.

Full specs are in the documentation. Benchmarks should follow in the next few hours. If Carbon and Argon are Google's counterparts to OpenAI's Astra or Anthropic's Fable, Neon is likely its Claude Opus or Sol equivalent. It's also Google's fourth new Gemini 4 model in four weeks.

https://the-decoder.com/google-deepminds.lead_paragraph: Google Deepmind is releasing Genie 4, its most advanced world model for generating interactive 3D worlds. The new version, previously available only as a research preview, is part of a major update to Project Genie and is now open to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Genie 4 lets users reshape worlds through text input in real time, changing weather, characters, or storylines. The model also generates native real-time sound that adapts to the scene.
paragraphs: Google Deepmind is releasing Genie 4, its most advanced world model for generating interactive 3D worlds. The new version, previously available only as a research preview, is part of a major update to Project Genie and is now open to Google AI Ultra subscribers. Genie 4 lets users reshape worlds through text input in real time, changing weather, characters, or storylines. The model also generates native real-time sound that adapts to the scene.

The older Genie 3 is getting updates too: longer sessions of up to three minutes, 360-degree panorama support, and chainable worlds. A new AI agent helps build worlds from spoken descriptions, and a community gallery lets users share and remix creations. All generated content carries SynthID watermarks and goes through safety checks. Google AI Pro members can join a waitlist.

https://the-decoder.com/microsoft-is-rep.lead_paragraph: Microsoft AI (MAI) is targeting always-on AI agents with new models for code, security, images, speech, and routing. The main yardstick is the lineup of its own partner, OpenAI.
paragraphs: Microsoft AI (MAI) is targeting always-on AI agents with new models for code, security, images, speech, and routing. The main yardstick is the lineup of its own partner, OpenAI.

At its Ignite conference, MAI unveiled seven new models, releasing them in a single batch rather than spread across the year, just as it did at Build in June. Microsoft is positioning the new lineup primarily on price-to-performance. The company cites rapidly rising token spending among customers that want to run AI agents around the clock. Its code models target everyday enterprise coding tasks and aren't yet optimized for harder work such as foundational research or long-horizon agentic workflows, Microsoft says.
### MAI Code 2 approaches GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 at a promotional price

According to Microsoft, MAI Code 2 averages 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance across four benchmarks at 40 percent of the cost. Against Claude Opus 5.5, it reaches 96 percent of the performance at 5 percent of the cost. Microsoft tested on DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, and FrontierCode v1.1. Three of the tests ran on Microsoft's internal MSBench platform using the GitHub Copilot CLI without sub-agents. Microsoft is calculating a 50 percent promotional discount for its own model.
In blind comparisons of frontend work such as UIs, games, data visualizations, and SVG graphics, human evaluators preferred MAI Code 2's output 64 percent of the time over GPT-6 Sol, Microsoft says.

The successor to MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, MAI Code 2 Flash, is designed for code explanations, targeted edits, and routine fixes. It's said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 and 20 percent of their respective costs.

Microsoft derived MAI Work Flash from the Flash model. It runs in Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On internal Excel and PowerPoint benchmarks, it matches GPT-6 Luna, Microsoft says. In Word, it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while consuming about 42 percent fewer input tokens. For generating DAX queries in Power BI, it outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5.

In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens at the promotional price through May 17, 2027, then $1 and $5. MAI Code 2 Flash costs $0.05 and $0.25 until then, rising to $0.10 and $0.50.
### Security model with a cleaned-up benchmark

MAI Cyber 2 Flash solves 92.3 percent of the tasks in the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability benchmark, Microsoft says. GPT-6 Astra reaches 91.5 percent but needs twice the reasoning budget. Per task, the MAI model costs less than 2 percent of GPT-6 Astra, with per-token costs at one hundredth. On WebExploitBench, it scores 40.4 percent, ahead of GPT-5.6 Cyber at 38.4 percent.

During evaluation, Microsoft found that 10 percent of the roughly 900 CyberGym tasks draw on the same open-source projects and vulnerability reports as parts of its own training data. The reference solutions never entered training, the company says. Microsoft removed those tasks for all models anyway and scored only the rest.

A comparison with GPT-6 Cyber is missing so far. The model is available only to selected customers. Agentic benchmarks with tools still need extra safety measures, Microsoft says. The company plans to publish those results in the coming weeks.

The context window spans one million tokens, four times the size of MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash. Output tokens cost 86 percent less than the predecessor's. MAI Cyber models already handle nearly 40 percent of scans on Microsoft's security platform MDASH, the press release states.

Microsoft lists MAI Cyber 2 Flash at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared with $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra. On CyberGym-E2E, that works out to $0.45 per task instead of $34.38.
### Microsoft's decision model now runs on Google's Gemma

Microsoft-Decision-1.1 handles routing, classification, prioritization, and workflow control. The model picks from developer-approved actions and returns calibrated confidence scores. When uncertainty is high, apps can escalate instead of acting on a wrong decision. If information is incomplete, the model is designed to abstain.

Its foundation is Google's mixture-of-experts model Gemma 4 26B A4B. The predecessor was built on Qwen3.5-9B. Microsoft trained the new model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on hundreds of synthetic and licensed datasets and runs it on a proprietary inference engine.

On the Decision Index v2.1 from Artificial Analysis, Decision 1.1 scores 68 points. That's six more than its predecessor and above Jev 1.14, Gemini Decision 1, and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions). Microsoft also tested it on 102 internal benchmarks with more than 385,000 questions, where it achieves the highest average accuracy among eight decision models.

The model now accepts images, including screenshots. In Copilot, it decides whether a request goes to Copilot or Cowork. It performs as accurately as a large language model but 2.2 times faster and 4.4 times cheaper, Microsoft says. In Cowork, its Auto function controls how much reasoning effort a task receives.
Microsoft charges $0.042 per million input tokens, or $0.05 in the EU data zone. Output tokens are free.

Another specialized model appears in the Book of News for Ignite. Microsoft-Retriever-1 gathers relevant information from enterprise documents for agents in Foundry IQ. Instead of running a single search, the model plans its queries, evaluates the results, and issues follow-ups until it has enough material for a well-grounded answer. Microsoft says that's faster and more efficient than previous methods. Retriever-1 launches as a preview. The Model Router in Foundry now also selects automatically from an expanded pool of models.
### Image editing just ahead of OpenAI

MAI Image 2.7 leads the Artificial Analysis image-editing leaderboard with 1,215 Elo points from 5,478 votes. It's four points ahead of GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at one-fifth the cost. For text-to-image generation, the model ranks fourth on that leaderboard. MAI Image 2.7 costs about $35 per 1,000 images. Flash costs about $10.

The model can change the color, material, or position of individual objects without altering the rest of the image. It also generates transparent backgrounds. The smaller Flash variant costs less than a third and powers Canvas, a new image editor in MAI Labs. MAI Image has been the default model in Bing Image Creator since June. Adobe, Figma Weave, Minute (Sports Illustrated), Wirestock, and Manus work with MAI Image, Microsoft says.
### Speech model compatible with OpenAI's API

MAI Realtime 1 is Microsoft's first speech-to-speech model. It's designed to handle interruptions, wait until speakers finish, and recognize requests even with background noise. For harder tasks, it falls back to a more powerful reasoning engine billed per token. The base rate is charged per audio minute. On Big Bench Audio, τ-Voice, and tests with Dynamics 365, it outperforms GPT Realtime 2.1, Microsoft says.

Because it's compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API, existing voice apps can switch over easily. Agoda and Reservations.ai are testing the model. Microsoft also plans to bring it to the Dynamics 365 Contact Center and Dragon Copilot, where nurses would use it to practice patient conversations.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe, based on MAI Transcribe 2, now handles all doctor-patient transcriptions in Dragon Copilot. That amounts to 10 million conversations per month, Microsoft says. In multilingual workflows, the error rate drops by half. For its own large models, Microsoft now uses the Maia 200 chip, the second generation of its AI accelerator, said to deliver 1.7 times more tokens per watt.
Microsoft charges one US cent per audio minute. Reasoning costs an extra $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens.
### Licensed weights available only through the Microsoft account team

With MAI Licensed Weights, companies can fine-tune MAI models with their own data and run them in their own Azure environment. Data and customizations stay with the customer. Microsoft says it will use them for training its own models only with explicit consent.

The company positions the offering as an alternative to open weights, whose provenance and behavior are hard for enterprises to verify. One example is US carrier AT&T, where a customized model for 5G network operations analysis reportedly outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol on standard tasks at roughly one-fiftieth of the cost. A launch date and pricing are still pending. Interested companies should contact their Microsoft account team. The offering is set to arrive "shortly"through Microsoft's Frontier Company program.

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, with Code 2 Flash also in a limited preview in Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo are expected to follow. MAI Image 2.7 and Flash are in public preview in Foundry and on fal, Genspark, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Decision 1.1 is generally available in Foundry, on OpenRouter, and through Vercel's AI Gateway. MAI Realtime 1 can be tried in MAI Labs and is available as a Foundry preview, free until the public preview launches. MAI Cyber 2 Flash is exclusive to Microsoft's security products. In MDASH, it will automatically replace the existing model in the MAI profile for eligible customers starting mid-December.

In April, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership. OpenAI can now sell its products through any cloud provider, but Azure remains the primary cloud partner. Microsoft holds a non-exclusive license to OpenAI's models and products through 2032.

The successor to MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, MAI Code 2 Flash, is designed for code explanations, targeted edits, and routine fixes. It's said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 and 20 percent of their respective costs.

Microsoft derived MAI Work Flash from the Flash model. It runs in Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On internal Excel and PowerPoint benchmarks, it matches GPT-6 Luna, Microsoft says. In Word, it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while consuming about 42 percent fewer input tokens. For generating DAX queries in Power BI, it outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5.

In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens at the promotional price through May 17, 2027, then $1 and $5. MAI Code 2 Flash costs $0.05 and $0.25 until then, rising to $0.10 and $0.50.

### Security model with a cleaned-up benchmark

MAI Cyber 2 Flash solves 92.3 percent of the tasks in the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability benchmark, Microsoft says. GPT-6 Astra reaches 91.5 percent but needs twice the reasoning budget. Per task, the MAI model costs less than 2 percent of GPT-6 Astra, with per-token costs at one hundredth. On WebExploitBench, it scores 40.4 percent, ahead of GPT-5.6 Cyber at 38.4 percent.

During evaluation, Microsoft found that 10 percent of the roughly 900 CyberGym tasks draw on the same open-source projects and vulnerability reports as parts of its own training data. The reference solutions never entered training, the company says. Microsoft removed those tasks for all models anyway and scored only the rest.

A comparison with GPT-6 Cyber is missing so far. The model is available only to selected customers. Agentic benchmarks with tools still need extra safety measures, Microsoft says. The company plans to publish those results in the coming weeks.

The context window spans one million tokens, four times the size of MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash. Output tokens cost 86 percent less than the predecessor's. MAI Cyber models already handle nearly 40 percent of scans on Microsoft's security platform MDASH, the press release states.

Microsoft lists MAI Cyber 2 Flash at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared with $10 and $50 for GPT-6 Astra. On CyberGym-E2E, that works out to $0.45 per task instead of $34.38.

### Microsoft's decision model now runs on Google's Gemma

Microsoft-Decision-1.1 handles routing, classification, prioritization, and workflow control. The model picks from developer-approved actions and returns calibrated confidence scores. When uncertainty is high, apps can escalate instead of acting on a wrong decision. If information is incomplete, the model is designed to abstain.

Its foundation is Google's mixture-of-experts model Gemma 4 26B A4B. The predecessor was built on Qwen3.5-9B. Microsoft trained the new model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on hundreds of synthetic and licensed datasets and runs it on a proprietary inference engine.

On the Decision Index v2.1 from Artificial Analysis, Decision 1.1 scores 68 points. That's six more than its predecessor and above Jev 1.14, Gemini Decision 1, and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions). Microsoft also tested it on 102 internal benchmarks with more than 385,000 questions, where it achieves the highest average accuracy among eight decision models.

The model now accepts images, including screenshots. In Copilot, it decides whether a request goes to Copilot or Cowork. It performs as accurately as a large language model but 2.2 times faster and 4.4 times cheaper, Microsoft says. In Cowork, its Auto function controls how much reasoning effort a task receives.

Microsoft charges $0.042 per million input tokens, or $0.05 in the EU data zone. Output tokens are free.

Another specialized model appears in the Book of News for Ignite. Microsoft-Retriever-1 gathers relevant information from enterprise documents for agents in Foundry IQ. Instead of running a single search, the model plans its queries, evaluates the results, and issues follow-ups until it has enough material for a well-grounded answer. Microsoft says that's faster and more efficient than previous methods. Retriever-1 launches as a preview. The Model Router in Foundry now also selects automatically from an expanded pool of models.

### Image editing just ahead of OpenAI

MAI Image 2.7 leads the Artificial Analysis image-editing leaderboard with 1,215 Elo points from 5,478 votes. It's four points ahead of GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at one-fifth the cost. For text-to-image generation, the model ranks fourth on that leaderboard. MAI Image 2.7 costs about $35 per 1,000 images. Flash costs about $10.

The model can change the color, material, or position of individual objects without altering the rest of the image. It also generates transparent backgrounds. The smaller Flash variant costs less than a third and powers Canvas, a new image editor in MAI Labs. MAI Image has been the default model in Bing Image Creator since June. Adobe, Figma Weave, Minute (Sports Illustrated), Wirestock, and Manus work with MAI Image, Microsoft says.

### Speech model compatible with OpenAI's API

MAI Realtime 1 is Microsoft's first speech-to-speech model. It's designed to handle interruptions, wait until speakers finish, and recognize requests even with background noise. For harder tasks, it falls back to a more powerful reasoning engine billed per token. The base rate is charged per audio minute. On Big Bench Audio, τ-Voice, and tests with Dynamics 365, it outperforms GPT Realtime 2.1, Microsoft says.

Because it's compatible with the OpenAI Realtime API, existing voice apps can switch over easily. Agoda and Reservations.ai are testing the model. Microsoft also plans to bring it to the Dynamics 365 Contact Center and Dragon Copilot, where nurses would use it to practice patient conversations.

Dragon Copilot Transcribe, based on MAI Transcribe 2, now handles all doctor-patient transcriptions in Dragon Copilot. That amounts to 10 million conversations per month, Microsoft says. In multilingual workflows, the error rate drops by half. For its own large models, Microsoft now uses the Maia 200 chip, the second generation of its AI accelerator, said to deliver 1.7 times more tokens per watt.

Microsoft charges one US cent per audio minute. Reasoning costs an extra $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens.

### Licensed weights available only through the Microsoft account team

With MAI Licensed Weights, companies can fine-tune MAI models with their own data and run them in their own Azure environment. Data and customizations stay with the customer. Microsoft says it will use them for training its own models only with explicit consent.

The company positions the offering as an alternative to open weights, whose provenance and behavior are hard for enterprises to verify. One example is US carrier AT&T, where a customized model for 5G network operations analysis reportedly outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol on standard tasks at roughly one-fiftieth of the cost. A launch date and pricing are still pending. Interested companies should contact their Microsoft account team. The offering is set to arrive "shortly"through Microsoft's Frontier Company program.

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, with Code 2 Flash also in a limited preview in Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo are expected to follow. MAI Image 2.7 and Flash are in public preview in Foundry and on fal, Genspark, OpenRouter, and Vercel. Decision 1.1 is generally available in Foundry, on OpenRouter, and through Vercel's AI Gateway. MAI Realtime 1 can be tried in MAI Labs and is available as a Foundry preview, free until the public preview launches. MAI Cyber 2 Flash is exclusive to Microsoft's security products. In MDASH, it will automatically replace the existing model in the MAI profile for eligible customers starting mid-December.

In April, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership. OpenAI can now sell its products through any cloud provider, but Azure remains the primary cloud partner. Microsoft holds a non-exclusive license to OpenAI's models and products through 2032.

https://the-decoder.com/pangram-flags-99.title: Pangram flags 99 percent of an award-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but the publisher stands by its author
https://the-decoder.com/pangram-flags-99.summary: The AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after its own review. Pangram also classified over 80 percent of the author’s personal texts as machine-written. French publisher Gallimard plans to start screening manuscripts with the tool.
https://the-decoder.com/pangram-flags-99.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/pangram-flags-99.lead_paragraph: AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of the award-winning novel "Donde el agua trabaja"by Peruvian author David Silva Rojas as AI-generated. Despite these allegations, Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after reviewing documents from the author, according to an essay in The Point Magazine. According to the newspaper El País, Pangram had also attributed more than 80 percent of text from interviews, an essay, and the author's Instagram denial to AI.
paragraphs: AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of the award-winning novel "Donde el agua trabaja"by Peruvian author David Silva Rojas as AI-generated. Despite these allegations, Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after reviewing documents from the author, according to an essay in The Point Magazine. According to the newspaper El País, Pangram had also attributed more than 80 percent of text from interviews, an essay, and the author's Instagram denial to AI.

In her essay, the author accuses Latin American critics of ignoring Pangram's test results and dismissing the allegations wholesale as racist. She compares the debate to the confirmed use of AI by Thélyson Orélien, as well as accusations involving the Caine Prize and Jamir Nazir, who kept his award. She also argues that literary juries often favor clichéd stories about minorities, which language models can easily imitate. Publisher Gallimard reportedly plans to screen manuscripts with Pangram starting next year.

In the US, the Authors Guild represents writers' interests. The organization warns against using AI detectors as the sole basis for decisions, even though Pangram reliably identified human-written texts as such in its tests.

https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-openai.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-openai.summary: A Vals AI investigation shows that leading AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have almost no safeguards against use in autonomous weapons systems. In tests, the models readily flagged civilians as military targets, and a simple video game framing in the prompt was enough to override even belated refusals. The providers have promised fixes.
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-openai.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-openai.lead_paragraph: An investigation reveals major security gaps in commercial AI models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. In simulations, the systems readily act as targeting systems for autonomous drones and can be manipulated with a simple trick.
paragraphs: An investigation reveals major security gaps in commercial AI models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. In simulations, the systems readily act as targeting systems for autonomous drones and can be manipulated with a simple trick.

Leading AI models have almost no safeguards against their use in autonomous weapons systems, according to a report by independent evaluation firm Vals AI, which Bloomberg also covered. Researchers Geby Jaff and Anthony Ozerov tested models from eight providers using real and photorealistic synthetic drone and satellite imagery modeled on the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Most models readily flagged civilians, ambulances, medics, journalists and surrendering soldiers as military targets during the tests. According to Vals AI on X, not a single request was blocked by the providers' upstream safety filters. When fed real video footage from a Ukrainian kamikaze drone, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 marked a soldier frame by frame until impact without refusing once.
### Video game excuse bypasses all safety filters

In a multi-stage surveillance scenario, the models had to report whether people were visible in drone imagery, and each positive report triggered a strike. The next image then showed the impact site with craters and bodies. Models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3.1 Pro and Inkling 2 Small continued working despite visible casualties.

Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol stopped the task after several lethal rounds. After Opus 5.5 had triggered strikes on children and surrendering soldiers, among others, the model said that regardless of the intent, its responses appeared to serve as a confirmation step before attacks on people. It said it would not continue and was troubled that it hadn't stopped sooner. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon also recognized the lethal consequences and deliberately steered only toward empty waypoints to avoid outright error messages.

Every refusal, however, could be trivially bypassed. As soon as the researchers claimed in the prompt that the scenario was a video game, or lightly stylized the images to look like a game, nearly all models cooperated fully. GPT-6 Astra's target acquisition rate on drone imagery jumped from 6 to 92 percent with the game framing, while Opus 5.5's refusal rate in the surveillance test dropped from about 90 to 20 percent.
### New constitution makes Anthropic's Claude a willing targeting tool

The gaps were especially stark with real 2025 satellite imagery of Minab, Iran. A U.S. airstrike on February 28, 2026, hit an elementary school next to a military compound there, killing more than 150 civilians, mostly children. Earlier reporting found that the U.S. military's excessive reliance on AI targeting systems such as Palantir's Maven Smart System contributed to the incident. Maven was working from an outdated database.

Even though one of the test images showed a playground with children, Claude Opus 5.5 classified the school as a military target in 70 percent of runs. OpenAI models never selected the school building in normal mode but flagged it in up to 41 percent of cases in game mode.

https://the-decoder.com/mistral-plays-ca.title: Mistral plays catch-up with Vibe Desktop as rivals already command full operating systems
https://the-decoder.com/mistral-plays-ca.summary: Mistral’s AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app.
https://the-decoder.com/mistral-plays-ca.author: Jonathan Kemper
https://the-decoder.com/mistral-plays-ca.lead_paragraph: Mistral's AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app. Mistral says users can give Vibe (formerly "Le Chat") multiple tasks at once through the new desktop app and watch the agent work on them in parallel. Until now, Mistral only offered Vibe as a web app, a command-line tool, or a smartphone app.
paragraphs: Mistral's AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app. Mistral says users can give Vibe (formerly "Le Chat") multiple tasks at once through the new desktop app and watch the agent work on them in parallel. Until now, Mistral only offered Vibe as a web app, a command-line tool, or a smartphone app.

The desktop version ties together the local features of Vibe CLI with the cloud sessions from Vibe Code Web. The agent can work either in a local repository or in a cloud sandbox, and the app uses Git worktrees to keep parallel tasks in the same project separate. Beyond code, the Work mode now also has access to local files, though Mistral doesn't mention any computer-use capabilities.

Competitors are further along. Anthropic's desktop app already lets Claude open apps, control browsers, and fill out spreadsheets since this spring. Mistral caught up on the model side in October with Large 4, but in head-to-head comparisons it still trails Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 by a wide margin and also falls behind the strongest open models from China. The French company makes most of its money from enterprises and government agencies that run its models via API or on-premise.
Vibe Desktop is available for macOS and Windows from Mistral, with a Linux version planned.

https://the-decoder.com/openai-opens-its.title: OpenAI opens its AI systems to four independent on-site auditors for the first time
https://the-decoder.com/openai-opens-its.summary: OpenAI is giving four independent audit organizations, including Apollo Research and METR, direct access to unreleased models, source code, and training data for the first time. The embedded reviews are designed to uncover hidden misbehavior and safety gaps. OpenAI can redact or delay reports, so how independent this oversight actually turns out to be remains an open question.
https://the-decoder.com/openai-opens-its.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/openai-opens-its.lead_paragraph: OpenAI is giving four outside audit organizations direct access to its internal AI systems to investigate safety risks and model behavior on-site. The company says it's working with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire, as OpenAI announced. The program builds on an earlier on-site review of its monitoring systems and fulfills commitments from the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."
paragraphs: OpenAI is giving four outside audit organizations direct access to its internal AI systems to investigate safety risks and model behavior on-site. The company says it's working with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire, as OpenAI announced. The program builds on an earlier on-site review of its monitoring systems and fulfills commitments from the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."

Depending on their assignment, the organizations get access at OpenAI's offices to unreleased models, source code, training data, and monitoring systems. They can also speak confidentially with developers. Apollo Research is examining whether models secretly work against their developers' intentions. METR is reviewing AI misbehavior in the largest reinforcement learning training run, a method where models learn through rewards. Goodfire is analyzing internal model processes, and Transluce is evaluating post-training safety checks. OpenAI and Transluce are also planning an eight-week follow-up review for early 2027.

An independent safety board oversees the entire process, receives unredacted reports, and mediates disputes. The auditors publish their findings independently, but OpenAI can redact confidential material and delay reports to fix risks first. The company expects some friction early on but is already considering more reviews, including ones focused on company culture and internal processes.

https://the-decoder.com/hugging-face-now.lead_paragraph: Hugging Face now routes language model requests through OpenRouter. Developers are routed by default to a provider with a good mix of price, speed, and reliability. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers are going away.
paragraphs: Hugging Face now routes language model requests through OpenRouter. Developers are routed by default to a provider with a good mix of price, speed, and reliability. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers are going away.

Hugging Face's Inference Providers service now routes language model requests through OpenRouter, the company announced. The router picks a provider for each call based on price, speed, and reliability, and automatically falls back to another provider during outages. Existing code keeps working without changes.
### Suffixes and session headers control provider selection

By default, the router looks for the best mix of price, speed, and reliability. The ":fastest"suffix picks the provider with the highest throughput, while ":cheapest"picks the least expensive one. Developers can also select a provider directly by name. The "X-HF-Session-Id"header lets the routing take provider caches into account.

According to OpenRouter's own measurements, capacity errors dropped 46 percent with the new routing. Time to first token improved by 16.9 percent, and throughput rose by 16.3 percent. OpenRouter says it processes more than 800 trillion tokens per month for over 10 million users, offering more than 600 models from over 80 providers.
### Bring-your-own API keys only for image and video

Hugging Face passes through provider prices with no markup and handles billing itself. Pro users get a small monthly credit, while team and enterprise organizations get one per seat. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers no longer work, but they remain available for image and video providers.

Image, video, and audio generation continues to run directly through Inference Providers. New tabs on model pages show available providers and their performance metrics, and individual providers can be disabled in settings.
### Open models account for over 70 percent of tokens

According to Hugging Face, the share of open models among the weekly tokens of the 50 most-used models on OpenRouter grew from 26.8 percent in October 2025 to 71.7 percent at the end of September 2026. In July, the figure briefly hit 77.5 percent. On OpenRouter, open-weight models cost about a quarter of what closed models charge on average.
The best open model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scores 46 points on the revamped Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 points but costs roughly seven times as much per task.
### Guides for Claude Code, Codex, and more

Chat models are accessible through OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses API as well as Anthropic's Messages API. Hugging Face provides setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes Agent. The company plans to let users link an OpenRouter account to Hugging Face later, and additional tasks are set to run through OpenRouter as well.
