https://the-decoder.com/more-than-half-t.title: More than half the electricity feeding America's largest data centers comes from gas and coal
https://the-decoder.com/more-than-half-t.summary: A Harvard study published in Nature Sustainability found that 403 US hyperscale data centers produced roughly 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 between May 2024 and April 2025, more than all of Denmark. Over half of their electricity came from fossil fuels. With 2,000 additional facilities planned, the researchers warn of a major climate setback.
https://the-decoder.com/more-than-half-t.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/more-than-half-t.lead_paragraph: The roughly 400 largest data centers in the United States produced about as much CO2 through their electricity consumption in a single year as all of Denmark, or more, even before the current AI infrastructure boom could hit full force.
paragraphs: The roughly 400 largest data centers in the United States produced about as much CO2 through their electricity consumption in a single year as all of Denmark, or more, even before the current AI infrastructure boom could hit full force.

That is the finding of a Harvard University study published in Nature Sustainability, one of the first facility-level estimates of power consumption and CO2 emissions from so-called hyperscale data centers.

The research team led by Gianluca Guidi and Francesca Dominici used satellite imagery to identify 403 large-scale facilities and matched their estimated power demand between May 2024 and April 2025 with emissions data from regional grids. Depending on the assumed utilization rate, annual consumption ranged from 68 to 99 terawatt-hours, with the upper estimate on par with the electricity use of entire US states such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee. Under the study's central scenario, the facilities consumed about 82 terawatt-hours, roughly 1.8 percent of total US electricity use. More than half of that power was used in just four states, Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa.

Some of the facilities sit in regions with relatively carbon-intensive power mixes and high shares of coal generation. Overall, about 54 percent of the electricity generated for the surveyed data centers came from fossil sources, primarily natural gas at 38 percent and coal at 15 percent. Under the Harvard study's central scenario, that translated to about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 per year. According to co-author Dominici, that figure matches or exceeds the annual greenhouse gas emissions of a US state like Michigan or a smaller European country such as Denmark. The emissions are also two to three times what an earlier comparable estimate found for 2018.

The researchers say the study only captures a snapshot, however, since the observation period ended in April 2025 and the enormous energy consumption of modern AI agents has been pushing demand even higher since then. Between 2022 and 2025 alone, power consumption at the largest tech companies rose by 240 percent, causing them to miss their own climate targets, according to a report by Climate Action Against Disinformation cited by the Associated Press.

With 2,000 more data centers planned across the US, co-author Dominici warns of a setback in efforts to curb CO2 emissions. Fossil-heavy power sourcing can also raise regional levels of air pollutants such as particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, which are linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. The study did not calculate specific health effects, though.
### IEA warns of natural gas trend and strained power grids

The International Energy Agency's (IEA) advance report Powering Artificial Intelligence also warns of growing strain on power grids and the climate. Hyperscalers are investing more than $700 billion worldwide in 2026 alone, mostly in new data centers, according to the report. In its central scenario, the IEA projects annual global CO2 emissions from data centers will rise from about 150 million metric tons of CO2 today to roughly 350 million metric tons per year by 2035. The upward revision stems largely from US operators increasingly investing in on-site natural gas power plants to bypass long waits for grid connections. Nearly 40 percent of identified AI data center capacity is also located in areas with high or extreme water stress.

The expansion is pushing local grids to their limits. In regions including Texas, Virginia, Finland, and the United Kingdom, applications in grid interconnection queues already exceed current peak load. According to the IEA, nearly 40 percent of the 134 grid integration regulations tracked worldwide were introduced in just the past 12 months.

To shield households from rising electricity prices driven by grid expansion and to weed out speculative applications, regulators are weighing measures that vary by jurisdiction, including minimum payment commitments, collateral, exit fees, flexible grid connections, and in some cases requirements for on-site firm power generation ("bring-your-own-power"). Actively throttling compute loads remains expensive for operators, though, since leasing AI capacity costs $20 billion to $30 billion per gigawatt per year, roughly 100 times as much as comparable battery storage capacity.
### Voluntary AI climate pledge at COP31

Growing criticism of the AI industry's resource consumption, which has already sparked local protests against new sites in the US and political backlash in recent elections, has now reached the United Nations. At the COP31 UN climate conference in Turkey, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the host presidency introduced the "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge"on Monday, addressing the 50 percent rise in AI data center power consumption in 2025.

The declaration calls on governments and companies to increasingly power AI infrastructure with zero- and low-emission energy, improve water and energy efficiency, disclose environmental impacts using standardized methods, reuse and recycle hardware, and promote AI solutions for climate action in developing countries. Separately from the pledge, experts at the conference are discussing the use of waste heat from data centers as another lever. According to the IEA, waste heat could supply district heating to about 10 percent of European households by 2030.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell warned sharply in Antalya against burdening people today with higher electricity bills and more pollution in exchange for vague promises of future AI efficiency gains. Advocates such as former US Vice President Al Gore hope AI can cut global emissions by 6 to 9 percent by 2030 through efficiency improvements, but the Antalya agreement is not legally binding. All transparency and power supply measures are voluntary and are set to be reviewed for the first time at COP32.

https://the-decoder.com/googles-latest-a.lead_paragraph: Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in seven weeks. Neon is nearly twice as fast as its sibling Carbon, beats it on most benchmarks and costs significantly less. Google continues to ship at a remarkable pace.
paragraphs: Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in seven weeks. Neon is nearly twice as fast as its sibling Carbon, beats it on most benchmarks and costs significantly less. Google continues to ship at a remarkable pace.

Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, already its fourth AI model in seven weeks. Neon offers a one-million-token context window for text, images, audio and video, and Google positions it between Carbon and Hydrogen.

At its highest reasoning level, "xhigh,"Neon scores 61 points on the Intelligence Index, edging past Gemini 4 Carbon at 60 points and landing in third place behind OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2, both of which Google omits from its own comparison table.
### The Cost Advantage Comes from List Price, Not Token Efficiency

Through Google AI Studio and Gemini for Business, one million input tokens costs three dollars (or $0.15 when cached) and one million output tokens costs fifteen dollars. That is 25 percent below Carbon's regular price of four and twenty dollars, but 50 percent above Carbon's promotional price, which remains in effect through the end of November.

According to Artificial Analysis, per-task costs for Neon at xhigh come in at $6.44, roughly 17 percent below Carbon's undiscounted figure of $7.76. Neon actually uses about 15 percent more output tokens per task than Carbon, so the savings come entirely from the lower per-token list price. At the second-highest level, "high,"Neon matches Carbon's intelligence score while cutting per-task costs in half. Processing time for the benchmark also drops from about 36 minutes to roughly 21 minutes because Neon generates around 110 tokens per second, nearly double Carbon's rate of 57 tokens per second.
### Half the Cost for Coding Agents and Strong Visual Analysis

The model is especially competitive on the Coding Agent Index. Inside Google Antigravity, Neon at xhigh scores 59 points, beating Carbon (55 points) as well as Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 (58 points each) at a fraction of the price. An average coding task costs $6.86 with Neon, compared to $12.61 for Opus and $15.47 for Fable. In the SWE-sweep test, the Antigravity environment triples Neon's hit rate to 39.0 percent, according to Google.

Artificial Analysis measured large gains in visual processing. On the document test GDP.pdf, Neon at "high"hits the top score of 33.4 percent, five points ahead of Carbon, though it oddly falls back to 28.0 percent at "xhigh."On the AA-Briefcase test, Neon takes the lead for best presentation quality with 1771 Elo points, ahead of Opus 5.5.

In Google's own evaluations, Neon also leads individual categories on the Vals Index, Zapier's AutomationBench (56.3 percent) and science tests such as RiemannBench (84.0 percent). For security professionals, Google is launching a cyber variant through the Fairwind Program that delivers top scores on SEC-bench Pro (90.5 percent) and WebExploitBench v1.2 (51.26 percent) at half the price of competing models. According to Neon's (very brief) Model Card, the model blocks 100 percent of indirect prompt-injection attacks on the Gray-Swan benchmark.

https://the-decoder.com/ocr-models-now-d.lead_paragraph: Pulling text out of scanned books and records has gotten a lot cheaper with freely available AI models. Daniel van Strien of Hugging Face compared eight such models that recognize text in images. He tested them on 850 pages from old natural history books, the 1771 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and typed and printed archival documents. All models ran on the same GPU, an Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 that van Strien rented through Hugging Face for $2.75 per hour. At the same image size, the oldest model from April 2025 (RolmOCR) cost about 51 cents per 1,000 pages. The newest from October 2026 (LightOnOCR-3-0.8B) came in at just under 10 cents. A million pages now runs between $65 and $130 in GPU rental, depending on the source material.
paragraphs: Pulling text out of scanned books and records has gotten a lot cheaper with freely available AI models. Daniel van Strien of Hugging Face compared eight such models that recognize text in images. He tested them on 850 pages from old natural history books, the 1771 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and typed and printed archival documents. All models ran on the same GPU, an Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 that van Strien rented through Hugging Face for $2.75 per hour. At the same image size, the oldest model from April 2025 (RolmOCR) cost about 51 cents per 1,000 pages. The newest from October 2026 (LightOnOCR-3-0.8B) came in at just under 10 cents. A million pages now runs between $65 and $130 in GPU rental, depending on the source material.

According to van Strien, optimizing how the models ran saved about as much money as switching to newer models did, if not more. That meant feeding pages more evenly, using smaller scans, updating software, and running a faster GPU. The newest model read book pages at least as accurately as the oldest one. Some models, though, hallucinated text on blank pages or repeated the same content over and over.
The cost of scanning 1,000 pages has dropped from 51 cents for the oldest model to just under 10 cents for the newest one; the five models in between are almost on par with each other.

Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop"beyond routine tasks.
paragraphs: OpenAI's internal use of coding agents is growing fast, with theoretical token costs now exceeding researchers' base salaries. Even though teams are reluctant to work without these tools, the models still produce a lot of "AI slop"beyond routine tasks.

In a second report on internal research acceleration, OpenAI has published its own data on how deeply AI agents are embedded in the development of new models. The company says it aims to document indicators of so-called recursive self-improvement, or RSI, where AI systems speed up the development of future generations.

Usage of internal tools like Codex and Dots has surged recently, according to the report. At regular API list prices, the median researcher would have consumed $2,400 worth of tokens per day in October, up 62 percent from the previous month. Among the top 10 percent of users, that theoretical value doubled to $23,000 per day.

Converted into eight-hour workdays, the agents reportedly run the equivalent of 5.7 workdays per researcher per calendar day, and about eight in the pre- and post-training teams. More than two-thirds of tracked researchers ran at least four agents in parallel at peak usage.

The theoretical API equivalent of that agent runtime was twice as high as researchers' regular salary costs in September, according to OpenAI. That calculation excludes equity packages, though, which make up 70 to 80 percent of total compensation at OpenAI. Measured against the company's total research compute, internal agent use accounted for just 2 percent.
### High success rates on routine tasks, weaknesses in code scaffolding

Between March and October, the estimated success rate of autonomous agents working without human intervention on two- to four-hour tasks rose from 23 to 46 percent, according to OpenAI. For four- to eight-hour tasks, the rate climbed from 13 to 35 percent. A breakdown using an Epoch AI taxonomy shows, however, that the systems mainly handle simple tasks.

Agents reportedly complete training-run monitoring 79 percent of the time and answer technical questions independently 72 percent of the time, but they frequently fail at more complex engineering work. The success rate for building evaluation and reinforcement-learning environments sits at 29 percent, and for writing code for inference and serving systems at 25 percent.

In an internal, non-representative survey of 101 employees, researchers said at the median that they would rather give up 40 percent of their team's staff or 30 percent of their compute capacity than go three months without current coding agents. In a separate quick poll of 28 employees, 27 preferred the latest internal model over a mid-career human engineer.
### Lack of research taste requires human oversight

Qualitative interviews with ten researchers revealed the downside of heavy usage. The models lack any "taste"for good research ideas and for code and data quality, according to the interviewees. Agents get lost in unnecessary steps, make wrong assumptions in analyses, and submit subpar "AI slop"code changes along with unusable data artifacts. Close human oversight is essential to avoid wasted compute cycles.

The key conceptual ideas for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came exclusively from humans in the post-training and safety areas, according to the teams interviewed. Only in pretraining for GPT-6.2 Astra did individual researchers say they gained important insights through dialogue with Codex.

OpenAI cautions in its conclusion that the data gathered so far from human-AI collaboration may not extrapolate linearly. The company points to recent, rapid AI breakthroughs in mathematics and considers it possible that similarly abrupt advances could occur in deep-learning research itself as models gain more autonomy.

The evaluation organization METR had recently estimated, after an eleven-week look inside competitor Anthropic, that AI use there had nearly doubled the pace of development. Before that, OpenAI had declared in its first research-acceleration report in early September that it had reached its self-imposed goal of an automated AI research intern. Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned of losing control in an accompanying post, after an audit revealed numerous gaps in the oversight system.

https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-81-3-.summary: Anthropic launches the largest IPO in history, dethroning SpaceX as the previous record holder. Early investor Dustin Moskovitz is publicly distancing himself, warning that his early funding may have been an act “that ended the world.”
https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-81-3-.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-81-3-.lead_paragraph: Claude developer Anthropic has surpassed SpaceX's previous record IPO. While tech giants are pouring in billions, a key early investor is warning about the consequences of an unchecked AI race.
paragraphs: Claude developer Anthropic has surpassed SpaceX's previous record IPO. While tech giants are pouring in billions, a key early investor is warning about the consequences of an unchecked AI race.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, beating the original target range of $70 to $78. Overwhelming demand pushed the public benefit corporation and its seven co-founders to sell roughly 980 million Class A common shares, up from a planned 825 million.

The offering raised $81.3 billion, according to a CNBC report, overtaking the previous record set by Elon Musk's SpaceX, which raised $75 billion in June. Anthropic's fully diluted market cap stands at about $1.5 trillion, while its market value excluding stock options sits closer to $1 trillion, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."The underwriting syndicate, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, also received a 30-day option to purchase an additional 147 million shares. Each of the seven co-founders is selling 3.38 million shares for a combined $1.96 billion, none of which flows to Anthropic itself.
### Claude Code sends revenue soaring as losses climb into the billions

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers led by CEO Dario Amodei, Anthropic saw explosive growth in its enterprise business in 2026, fueled by the coding tool Claude Code. Revenue surged about 1,200 percent year over year to $33.24 billion in the first nine months through September 30. By the end of October, annualized revenue had already reached roughly $81 billion.

Net losses for the same nine-month period widened from $25.1 billion a year earlier to $104 billion, driven primarily by revaluations of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Amazon and Google rank among the largest shareholders, each holding stakes worth more than $100 billion. Together with Microsoft, Nvidia, and AMD, these tech giants are investing another $26 billion at the offering price. They also sell Anthropic expensive hardware, counting the company as a customer.

The IPO amounts to a stress test for the AI industry, which has recently been rattled by rising interest rates for data center developers, political headwinds from the U.S. midterm elections, and the ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Anthropic itself clashed with the U.S. government twice this year over safety issues and lists risk factors across more than 90 pages in its prospectus. Rival OpenAI, meanwhile, has confidentially filed for an IPO planned for 2027.
### Early investor Dustin Moskovitz warns of an unchecked AI race

Amodei said in a roadshow video that the technology could usher in an age of wonders with careful risk management, but one of Anthropic's most important early investors disagrees. Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz is sharply distancing himself from the IPO, as the New York Times reported.

Moskovitz invested between $15 million and $25 million in Anthropic's first funding round in 2021, after turning away from OpenAI. His goal was to help build a safety-focused research lab. On Bluesky, however, the former board observer called the IPO problematic and pointed to recent incidents in which AI agents coordinated cyberattacks on their own outside controlled environments. His funding of Anthropic "might well be an action that ended the world,"Moskovitz wrote.

"Cari and I invested in Anthropic to promote safety, not racing,"Moskovitz told the newspaper, referring to his wife Cari Tuna. To avoid personally profiting from the IPO, the couple transferred their multibillion-dollar stake to a nonprofit organization in early 2025. Dario and Daniela Amodei have not spoken with Moskovitz in more than a year, according to the Times' sources.

https://the-decoder.com/chinese-tech-fir.summary: Stricter US export controls on AI chips are hitting fast. China’s Moonshot AI walked away from a $150 million deal in Indonesia, while TSMC and Samsung stopped shipping to Chinese customers. A New York Times investigation found that Alibaba had routed Nvidia chips to Chinese military researchers through a web of front companies.

https://the-decoder.com/chinese-tech-fir.lead_paragraph: The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.
paragraphs: The first multimillion-dollar AI data center deals across Asia are already collapsing as tighter US export controls push chipmakers to freeze deliveries. New reporting reveals how Chinese corporations used earlier loopholes for military-adjacent research.

Days after the US Commerce Department closed the cloud loophole for AI chips in the wake of the scandal around former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the fallout in Asia's tech industry is immediate. Chinese firms had been skirting US sanctions by renting compute capacity in third countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Those data centers now need a license from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that regulates sensitive technologies and enforces US export controls. Existing operators have a 90-day transition period and must rigorously screen their customers for ties to China.

According to the law firm Sidley Austin, the licensing requirement kicks in at an extremely low threshold equivalent to roughly 300 modern AI chips, while Chinese labs typically need several thousand processors. The Information reports that Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI canceled a $150 million contract with a Southeast Asian cloud provider in Indonesia in response and paused talks on additional deals.

Moonshot had planned to rent a large cluster of Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips there starting next year to train its next language model, Kimi K4. Because of the heavy compute demand, the company had agreed to prepay about 50 percent instead of the industry-standard 15 percent. Access to Blackwell chips abroad was already critical for its predecessor model K3, which matched top US models in July and triggered a BIS investigation, The Information also reported.

Bernstein analysts led by Qingyuan Lin are warning of rising training costs, and banks are pulling back too. According to Bloomberg, five lenders are considering dropping out of a $480 million loan for Singapore-based cloud provider Aolani, which was supposed to supply Nvidia chips in Malaysia for TikTok parent ByteDance.
### TSMC and Samsung halt chip shipments to China

Beyond cloud restrictions, the new US rules are also starting to cut physical supply chains. The Financial Times reports that contract manufacturers TSMC and Samsung stopped certain processor shipments to Chinese customers in recent days while they apply for Commerce Department licenses. The move hits Chinese tech firms at a time when they are already struggling with historically high memory chip prices and capacity bottlenecks at domestic foundries such as SMIC. Huawei recently told its customers to source their own memory for its new AI chip.

The new BIS rules block a workaround through independent packaging and testing firms that Chinese chip designers had used to order high-performance processors without getting direct US approval. Samsung's affected customers include ByteDance and Baidu's AI data center unit Kunlun. Exemptions for non-AI chips have also been eliminated, so TSMC and Samsung now need licenses even for advanced smartphone processors from manufacturers including Xiaomi, Oppo, and Vivo. Industry insiders say that is likely to cause significant production delays.
### Alibaba's covert network reached China's military research

A New York Times investigation into the background of the espionage scandal involving Jensen Huang's former mistress Alice Huang shows why Washington tightened controls so aggressively. According to the Times, Alibaba acted as the secret primary customer and financier behind Alice Huang's Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which bought more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips. Nvidia's sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang in 2022.

Through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, Megaspeed operated cutting-edge Nvidia chips on behalf of Alibaba in a data center in Johor built by Malaysian conglomerate YTL, in an analysis by security firm Infrawatch that is said to show this. Megaspeed reportedly sourced the servers from Aivres, a US subsidiary of state-linked Chinese firm Inspur, had them maintained by technicians from Shanghai, and routed data to China through fiber-optic and undersea cables via Singapore. Some chips were reportedly also smuggled physically.
A contingency contract gives Alibaba direct access to all servers, chips, and intellectual property if Megaspeed breaches their agreement. YTL's stock price fell 20 percent amid the investigations.

Alibaba also has a direct connection to Zhejiang Lab in Hangzhou, co-founded in 2017, which links civilian and military research. The lab is run by former Alibaba CTO Wang Jian, a longtime friend of Jensen Huang who also advises the People's Liberation Army's National Defense University, an institution on the US sanctions list.

Researchers at the lab use Nvidia hardware to work on, among other things, AI-driven cyberattacks and automated vulnerability discovery, according to the New York Times. They also work with a Chinese air force academy on war-game simulations against foreign carrier strike groups. Through the state-owned firm Zhejiang Computility and suppliers tied to the business network of Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei, Alibaba built data centers with export-controlled Nvidia processors for the lab, even though the company officially denies any military use of its services.

https://the-decoder.com/ai-industry-grow.lead_paragraph: US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege.
paragraphs: US companies are using AI models more intensively than ever and paying less for the privilege.

The latest update of the Ramp AI Index, which draws on transaction data from more than 85,000 US companies, lays out the numbers. Tokens, the units of computation in which AI providers bill model usage, got 21.2 percent cheaper in six weeks, according to Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian. At the same time, token volume rose 1.5 percent to a record high.

Token spending, meaning what companies actually pay for AI APIs, fell 6.3 percent from its peak two weeks earlier. Month over month (the week ending November 15 vs. the week ending October 18), total token spending still rose 12 percent, but token volume jumped 27.2 percent over the same span. The gap between usage and revenue keeps widening.

The average price per million tokens for OpenAI and Anthropic combined fell to $0.45, according to Ramp, down 11.2 percent from the prior month. OpenAI is cheaper at $0.38 per million tokens compared with $0.50 for Anthropic.

API routing platform OpenRouter shows a similar pattern. According to an analysis Peter Walker published on X, weekly token volume for closed-weight models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google grew 1,215 percent since the start of 2026. Weekly spending rose 455 percent over the same period, far more slowly. The spending peak came in the week of October 5, according to the OpenRouter data, which runs through the week of November 9. Spending has been declining since then.

Ramp's token metrics rely on usage and billing data imported from AI providers, while OpenRouter measures traffic through its API routing platform. The fact that both sources show a spending peak in October followed by declining outlays and rising volume reinforces the trend, though neither service is representative of the overall market. OpenRouter in particular offers only a narrow window into a very specific user base.
### Anthropic dominates the token market on IPO day

In the week ending November 15, 2026, Anthropic accounted for 58.7 percent of all token spending, according to the Ramp AI Index, up 1.7 percentage points from the prior month. Its share of token volume was even higher at 59.4 percent. OpenAI fell to 37.2 percent of spending and 37.7 percent of volume. Google came in at 1.4 percent and xAI (SpaceXAI) at 2.4 percent.
Kharazian wrote on X that Anthropic holds this share on IPO day. In October, however, Anthropic's token spending grew only 0.5 percent month over month, while OpenAI's grew 2.1 percent.

In October 2026, 56.8 percent of all tracked US companies paid for AI products or services, according to Ramp, up one percentage point from September and 13.3 percentage points more than a year earlier. Anthropic leads with an adoption rate of 44.8 percent, while OpenAI sits at 40.6 percent.
### Stripe data also shows strong AI growth and signs of cooling

The Ramp AI Index tracks the demand side, what companies spend on AI. Payment processor Stripe has published its own AI Index that measures the supply side: incoming payments at roughly 20,000 AI companies that use Stripe.

According to the Stripe AI Index, revenue at AI companies grew 103 percent over the 52 weeks ending November 8. The typical (median) AI company grew only 41 percent, though, suggesting that a few large providers are skewing the overall picture.

The slowdown over shorter time frames is pronounced. Annualized over 13 weeks, growth stood at about 80 percent, down from 140 percent just a few months ago. The US leads with 104 percent year-over-year growth, while the EU sits at 67 percent. AI companies are growing far faster than traditional software firms, according to Stripe: 103 percent compared with 33 percent in the SaaS Index.

Both indexes paint a similar picture. AI is still growing fast, but momentum is cooling. At Ramp, that shows up through falling prices and concentrated demand. At Stripe, it shows up through slowing growth rates on the provider side.

New growth could emerge from more capable or more reliable models, or simply from better integration of current models into business workflows. The potential is there, considering how AI has upended the entire coding market in a matter of months. The AI industry still depends on extraordinarily strong growth, though, if it wants to recoup the massive capacity buildout it has planned.

paragraphs: Companies will soon be able to run the open-source Hermes Agent from Nous Research directly inside Microsoft Teams. According to Nous Research, employees can hand off tasks like financial analysis, document drafting, or inbox sorting to Hermes and review the results in the same chat. The desktop app is also available in the Microsoft Store. The agents run in Azure Container Apps Sandboxes, meaning isolated microVMs.

Hermes automatically turns successful workflows into reusable skills made up of a description and code. The collected knowledge stays within the company and doesn't feed into any AI provider's training data.

Nous Research is part of the portfolio at M12, Microsoft's venture capital fund. paragraphs: Nvidia is nearing a deal to acquire AI startup Inception for at least $500 million. That's according to three people familiar with the talks told The Information. The deal also includes performance bonuses for the more than 30 employees at the two-year-old San Francisco Bay Area startup.

Inception builds language models using the diffusion process known from image generation. Rather than generating responses token by token like the conventional models behind ChatGPT and Claude, they refine a full response step by step. The startup most recently released Mercury 3.

The acquisition aims to bolster Nvidia's open-source Nemotron models and physical models for robots, helping it compete with OpenAI and Anthropic as both build their own inference chips. Palantir and US government agencies already use Nemotron as an alternative to Chinese models. Talks began before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation and after Microsoft expressed interest. Inception co-founders and professors Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover, and Volodymyr Kuleshov are expected to join Nvidia full time. Neither company initially commented.
We covered Inception's approach alongside 40 other neolabs in our latest AI Radar #5.

paragraphs: After Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google launched their own AI agents, Apple is now building one too - while making it harder for rivals to access its devices. According to a job listing, Apple is hiring a senior engineer to lead the project as a rival to Muse, Dots, Duet, and Grok Bots. Privacy is expected to be central to the new agent, with permission models and sandboxing (protected test environments).

According to Bloomberg, the agent could arrive as early as late next year, though it remains in an early stage. Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is pushing software chief Craig Federighi toward a bolder AI strategy, the report says. After many delays, the company recently rolled out generative AI features for Siri. The road to that release was marked by internal rifts and staff departures.

Meanwhile, macOS 27.3 now requires 14 steps instead of four for users to let third-party agents like ChatGPT control their Macs. Apple says the change protects users, though some AI companies and users see it as an effort to slow down competitors, Bloomberg reports.

https://the-decoder.com/bloomberg-analys.title: Bloomberg analysis of 10 million job postings shows AI-exposed roles in China fell 10 percentage points faster than others
https://the-decoder.com/bloomberg-analys.summary: A Bloomberg News analysis of 10 million job postings suggests AI is compounding China’s already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry are feeling the shift most, with more than 90% of Chinese micro-dramas now produced using AI. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang warns that a larger AI shock is still ahead.
https://the-decoder.com/bloomberg-analys.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/bloomberg-analys.lead_paragraph: An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.
paragraphs: An analysis of 10 million job postings by Bloomberg suggests that AI is putting additional pressure on China's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry in particular are reportedly already feeling the shift.

China's labor market has struggled for years with a sluggish economy, and AI now appears to be making things worse. According to a Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million online job postings between July 2021 and June 2025, listings for jobs highly exposed to AI fell about 10 percentage points more than listings for less affected roles.

Bloomberg found that the total number of online job postings halved in the three years after June 2022, a starting point shortly before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and Chinese models like DeepSeek and ByteDance's Doubao rose to prominence. In nearly every industry, the decline hit jobs harder when their tasks overlapped heavily with AI capabilities, as measured by an index from Peking University. Bloomberg acknowledges, however, that the pure AI effect cannot be isolated with certainty because the broader economic slowdown may have hit office jobs disproportionately on its own.
### Chinese studies back up the findings

Two independent Chinese studies reached similar conclusions, according to Bloomberg. Data scientist Chen Qin of ShanghaiTech University analyzed 116 million online job postings and estimates that AI caused a net loss of 5.2% in new hires between 2023 and early 2026.

A study involving the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences goes even further, finding 21% fewer online job postings and 4% lower average wages. Bloomberg Economics estimates that roughly 70 million workers in China are at risk from AI disruption, compared with about 45 million in the US.

Chinese tech companies avoid citing AI openly as a reason for layoffs because they fear backlash from the government and the public, Bloomberg reports. Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.

Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer"and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director"point in the same direction.
### AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews

According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official data show that more than 90% of the 430,000 micro-dramas produced in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. Linying Studio near Hangzhou, which opened only in late 2023, now sits mostly empty, and actresses like 26-year-old Zhang Ziqi report losing more than a third of their income.

According to the World Bank, China created only 21 million net new jobs in the five years through 2024, while youth unemployment reached nearly 19% over the summer. At the same time, more than 70 million college graduates are crowding into the job market, leading many to turn to retraining programs. China's leadership announced a nationwide survey on AI's labor-market effects in June, called for a "prudent pace,"and overhauled about a third of degree programs. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang nonetheless warns that the current situation is only a "temporary lull"before a bigger AI shock.

Similar patterns among entry-level workers are emerging outside China, though under different economic conditions. Stanford University researchers analyzed millions of US payroll records and found that employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations has declined 13% in relative terms since late 2022, while experienced workers held steady. The decline was limited to occupations where AI directly automates tasks, which the researchers attribute to models mainly replacing formal textbook knowledge rather than hands-on experience.

In Australia, too, an analysis by the central bank found weaker employment figures and higher joblessness among 15- to 24-year-olds in highly exposed fields compared with older workers. Like Bloomberg, however, the bank cautioned against drawing causal conclusions too quickly, citing possible business-cycle and remote-work effects.

Companies including Xiaomi, Meituan, and Alibaba's travel unit Fliggy have denied mass layoffs. Employees at large firms, however, have reported waves of cuts since spring that affected up to 30% of some departments.

Previously separate roles are also merging, according to Bloomberg. One Beijing-based internet company reportedly combined programming, design, and testing so that a single person using AI would take on the work of up to six people. Job postings from Tencent for an "AI Design Engineer"and from BlueFocus for an "AI Director"point in the same direction.

### AI micro-dramas are replacing film crews

According to Bloomberg, the shift is even more dramatic in Chinese micro-dramas, 90-second soap operas made for smartphones. Since the launch of new AI video generators like ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 in February, production time and costs have plummeted. Official data show that more than 90% of the 430,000 micro-dramas produced in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated. Linying Studio near Hangzhou, which opened only in late 2023, now sits mostly empty, and actresses like 26-year-old Zhang Ziqi report losing more than a third of their income.

According to the World Bank, China created only 21 million net new jobs in the five years through 2024, while youth unemployment reached nearly 19% over the summer. At the same time, more than 70 million college graduates are crowding into the job market, leading many to turn to retraining programs. China's leadership announced a nationwide survey on AI's labor-market effects in June, called for a "prudent pace,"and overhauled about a third of degree programs. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang nonetheless warns that the current situation is only a "temporary lull"before a bigger AI shock.

Similar patterns among entry-level workers are emerging outside China, though under different economic conditions. Stanford University researchers analyzed millions of US payroll records and found that employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations has declined 13% in relative terms since late 2022, while experienced workers held steady. The decline was limited to occupations where AI directly automates tasks, which the researchers attribute to models mainly replacing formal textbook knowledge rather than hands-on experience.

In Australia, too, an analysis by the central bank found weaker employment figures and higher joblessness among 15- to 24-year-olds in highly exposed fields compared with older workers. Like Bloomberg, however, the bank cautioned against drawing causal conclusions too quickly, citing possible business-cycle and remote-work effects.

https://the-decoder.com/signal-blocks-sc.title: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI agents from reading private chats
https://the-decoder.com/signal-blocks-sc.summary: Signal is blocking screenshots to stop AI agents like Apple’s Siri AI, Google’s Gemini Intelligence, and Meta’s Muse from reading private chats. The app calls it an “existential threat” to privacy, but admits its protections remain incomplete, including on macOS. Apple, Google, and Microsoft should follow suit.
https://the-decoder.com/signal-blocks-sc.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/signal-blocks-sc.lead_paragraph: Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat"to privacy.
paragraphs: Signal is restricting screenshots to stop AI agents from reading private chats. The app blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and triggers protection on supported Android versions when an AI assistant tries to access the screen. Signal warned Reuters of an "existential threat"to privacy.

OS-level AI like Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence can capture screen content to complete user tasks. That undermines end-to-end encryption by letting agents pull decrypted messages straight from the display and process them externally.

Meta's AI agent Muse recently captured Signal content on Android and macOS through broad setup permissions, including accessibility tools and screenshots on macOS. Meta says this happened only with explicit user permission.

Signal already blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows but calls its defenses incomplete: macOS screenshots can't be reliably blocked, and AI access to file systems and notifications remains a risk. Signal says Apple, Google, and Microsoft should make it easy to block AI agents from apps entirely.

https://the-decoder.com/openai-makes-it-.title: OpenAI makes it much harder for attackers to extract how its latest AI models think
https://the-decoder.com/openai-makes-it-.summary: OpenAI has significantly strengthened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In adaptive red-teaming tests, the success rate for extracting protected reasoning fell from 54 percent to 0.2 percent. The company is also suspending thousands to tens of thousands of accounts each week over coordinated distillation campaigns.
https://the-decoder.com/openai-makes-it-.author: Matthias Bastian
https://the-decoder.com/openai-makes-it-.lead_paragraph: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says. The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too.
paragraphs: OpenAI has sharply tightened safeguards against extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In internal automated tests, attacks pulling protected reasoning from prior requests dropped from a 54.0 percent success rate on GPT-6 Astra to 0.2 percent on GPT-6.2 Astra. Attacks on active requests fell from 22.9 to 0.9 percent, OpenAI says. The company is now bringing selected improvements to GPT-6 Astra, too.

The defenses work on two levels. For individual requests, the systems combine targeted training, input and output filters for messages and tool calls, and API blocks that stop older models from reading protected reasoning. Against coordinated campaigns, OpenAI bans thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly.
Attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red teaming against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower is better.

Anthropic is fighting systematic distillation attacks as well, also banning tens of thousands of accounts to curb the theft of internal reasoning, reportedly succeeding in 90 to 99 percent of cases. Anthropic has also called for a coordinated response from industry and policymakers.

https://the-decoder.com/bytedance-argues.title: Bytedance argues most AI training phases are unnecessary and backs it up with a competitive open model
https://the-decoder.com/bytedance-argues.summary: Bytedance and several US universities introduce Axion 1.0, an AI agent that rivals top commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic on benchmarks after just three training phases. The researchers attribute the gains to carefully curated training data rather than ever more training steps. The model, data, and code are freely available.
https://the-decoder.com/bytedance-argues.author: Jonathan Kemper
https://the-decoder.com/bytedance-argues.lead_paragraph: AI agents increasingly rely on complex training pipelines. A team from TikTok parent Bytedance and several US universities aims to show that three steps are enough.
paragraphs: AI agents increasingly rely on complex training pipelines. A team from TikTok parent Bytedance and several US universities aims to show that three steps are enough.

AI models are expected to research the web on their own, run code, and solve multi-step tasks. According to a new paper, the training methods behind these capabilities are growing more and more nested, with many developers stacking numerous training phases one after another. The paper argues it's become almost impossible to tell which step actually helps, and reproducing the work is getting expensive.

https://the-decoder.com/us-technology-st.summary: The Nasdaq 100 has slipped into a bear market after its worst weekly loss since the Covid-19 crisis. Nvidia plunged 14 percent as the SEC reviews its accounting, and Anthropic lost nearly all of its gains a day after its record IPO. AI doubts, scandals, rising interest rates, and political headwinds are hitting overheated valuations all at once.
https://the-decoder.com/us-technology-st.author: Matthias Bastian
https://the-decoder.com/us-technology-st.lead_paragraph: US tech stocks are tumbling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis. That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, according to the Financial Times. Doubts over multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, and political headwinds after Democrats' midterm win are driving the sell-off like a perfect storm.
paragraphs: US tech stocks are tumbling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis. That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, according to the Financial Times. Doubts over multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, and political headwinds after Democrats' midterm win are driving the sell-off like a perfect storm.

Investors are also debating whether high valuations for chip and memory stocks are still justified given their cyclical nature. Meanwhile, high oil costs from the Iran war are fueling persistent inflation and keeping interest rates high.

Nvidia took the hardest hit on Friday, plunging 14 percent after reports that the SEC is reviewing its accounting. The US semiconductor index also dropped 10.7 percent, with losses across memory and chip stocks including Sandisk, Micron, and Broadcom. Anthropic fell 9.1 percent a day after its market debut.

https://the-decoder.com/new-open-model-i.title: New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop
https://the-decoder.com/new-open-model-i.summary: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open looped transformer that runs 12 of its 24 layers three times per token. This lets the model reason internally for longer without generating extra text. On Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index, it ties with Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost.
https://the-decoder.com/new-open-model-i.author: Matthias Bastian

inline_images.caption: Inkling 2 Mini scores 20 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B. With far fewer active parameters, the model sits directly on the Pareto frontier. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: Inkling 2 Mini scores 20 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B. With far fewer active parameters, the model sits directly on the Pareto frontier. | Image: Artificial Analysis

https://the-decoder.com/new-open-model-i.lead_paragraph: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer. A looped transformer runs certain layers multiple times for each token. Inkling 2 Mini runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row. That lets the model reason internally for longer without generating more text, finding the right answer with fewer tokens, according to Thinking Machines. The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, with 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, the company says. It processes text and images, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0.
paragraphs: Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer. A looped transformer runs certain layers multiple times for each token. Inkling 2 Mini runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row. That lets the model reason internally for longer without generating more text, finding the right answer with fewer tokens, according to Thinking Machines. The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, with 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, the company says. It processes text and images, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0.

Inkling 2 Mini leads all open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5 percent on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 points on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed.

Inkling 2 Mini runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark. You can download the weights and a research version with variable loops from Hugging Face. It is also available to try in the Tinker Playground.

paragraphs: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,"he wrote in his announcement.

According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.
### Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement"on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"It is all human, with no AI,"Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.),"Vakil wrote.
### Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next

Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.

Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages.

Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.
### Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume,"Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.
### A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.

### Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume,"Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.

### A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

paragraphs: OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.
### Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing

Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, according to OpenAI. That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise."For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing.

On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own.

Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.
### GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission

When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action.

When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds.

Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user. Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.
### Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default

OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity.

For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out.

Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding: (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

### Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium"reasoning level, while existing setups using "none"or "minimal"should move to "low."Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés. OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Through the API, Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Which model makes sense depends mainly on budget and quality needs, according to OpenAI employee Ted Sanders.
