paragraphs: A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.
Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries.

According to Kriss's New Yorker report, about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.
### Maple's answer to "dataism"puts residents under strict control

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism"as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote.

Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress.
### Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall

Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores."Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores."One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans."
Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering.

Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned"AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing.

According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god."

Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy."
### Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns
According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely.

Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales"about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions.

Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community.

Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies,"especially in its early years.
### Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults

Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future."According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely."

Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically."Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence.

That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future,"to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious. When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess.
On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.
### Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit shows how widespread extinction fears are among AI researchers

Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon also fears that AI could lead to human extinction. After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet.

He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average. Coxon points to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress, though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Such warnings have also drawn sharp criticism from other researchers. Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse"hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation. AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term.
The industry's turn to religious advisers has critics, too. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power, and control.

In tests, periodic summaries and targeted keyword search usually matched full-context results at a fraction of the cost. The team even proposes a new class of models that works with short notes instead of long context.

https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-an.lead_paragraph: An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.
paragraphs: An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X.
### Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5. The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max"model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.
Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.
### Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.
The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.

https://the-decoder.com/lean-and-mathlib.lead_paragraph: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.
paragraphs: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.

The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.

The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

https://the-decoder.com/security-researc.summary: Security researchers at Dragos used two million fake AI requests to uncover serious vulnerabilities in the AI supply chain, finding at least three compromised providers, hundreds of stolen AWS keys, and marketplace resellers who were simply reading customer requests. OpenRouter responded by removing three providers and 125 endpoints.
https://the-decoder.com/security-researc.author: Matthias Bastian

inline_images.caption: OpenRouter's email warns affected users that third parties may have read their requests to MiniMax models. | Image: Jonathan Kemper

https://the-decoder.com/security-researc.lead_paragraph: Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.
paragraphs: Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.
Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.
### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.

Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.

### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.

A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.

But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

https://the-decoder.com/ai-is-getting-be.lead_paragraph: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.
paragraphs: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

https://the-decoder.com/perplexitys-new-.lead_paragraph: Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.
paragraphs: Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.
### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.
### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-so.title: GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy
https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-so.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra independently produced a machine-verifiable Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s gap theorem, the first of its kind according to Vals AI. The model chose its own approach because key foundations were missing from Mathlib. On Autoform-Hard, Astra now leads the leaderboard with 49 of 56 tasks solved.
https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-so.author: Manuel Uth

inline_images.caption: GPT-6.2 Astra built its proof around "capacity,"a metric that behaves like the edge of a graph. | Image: Vals AI
inline_images.caption_en: GPT-6.2 Astra built its proof around "capacity,"a metric that behaves like the edge of a graph. | Image: Vals AI

https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-so.lead_paragraph: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI, it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean. The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs, Vals says. It used "capacity,"a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step.
paragraphs: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI, it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean. The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs, Vals says. It used "capacity,"a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step.

This happened on Autoform-Hard, a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each.

Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs, Vals says. It used "capacity,"a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step.

This happened on Autoform-Hard, a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each.

paragraphs: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely considered the most intellectually demanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The brightest minds have failed to crack it for 150 years. The fact that an AI model played a major role in the breakthrough shows that raw intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, Wang argues.

According to Wang, current models only lack domain-specific knowledge and practical infrastructure to outperform humans in nearly every field. That includes AI research itself. Since AI research is intellectually less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis, Wang believes models could soon automate their own development and improve themselves. They could also dramatically speed up biological research, weapons research, and economic research at a pace humans can barely follow.

Wang also warns that the AI industry isn't thinking hard enough about what comes next. In his view, many in the field treat superintelligence as inevitable and focus only on safety. But the stakes are much broader than that, he argues. The industry needs to actively ensure that AI gives people more agency rather than taking control of society. That would require a sharp departure from the current course, Wang says. Despite having its own superintelligence team, Meta isn't a major player at the frontier right now.

paragraphs: The woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal was in contact with China's top spy agency for over a year, US intelligence reports show. Alice Huang communicated with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 through this fall, according to the New York Times, citing US intelligence findings. The entire time, she was carrying on a secret affair with then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

US spy agencies had been tracking the contacts for more than a year. Alice Huang's business partner Kang Wei, whom she introduced to acquaintances as her husband, is also believed to have cooperated with the ministry. Federal investigators are now trying to determine whether the two used a web of companies across Southeast Asia to funnel Nvidia AI chips into China, skirting US export controls. Alice Huang's firm Megaspeed is part of that network.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month after the affair became public, along with reports of a second relationship. President Donald Trump tried to downplay the allegations and floated the idea of Huang returning to the company. Nvidia's board shut that down.

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Nvidia to come clean about its chip sales to China before the company makes any decisions about its future leadership. Jensen Huang is set to testify behind closed doors before the US House of Representatives on December 1.

Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. That would undermine China's deterrence strategy, which relies on a guaranteed second-strike capability.
paragraphs: Chinese military researchers fear that AI advances could give the US an edge in the nuclear balance of power. Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. That would undermine China's deterrence strategy, which relies on a guaranteed second-strike capability.

Researchers at the Academy of Military Sciences in Beijing write that AI could shrink US decision-making time from 15 to 30 minutes down to 90 seconds. China currently has about 620 operational warheads, according to the Federation of American Scientists, and is expected to expand its arsenal to roughly 1,000 by 2030. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are studying how AI could make their own weapons harder to intercept, for instance by using AI-controlled flight paths for hypersonic missiles.

Experts warn, however, that flawed AI data could trigger dangerous miscalculations during a crisis. That risk proved very real earlier this year, when the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship based on a false, AI-generated intelligence report. Xi Jinping did discuss nuclear risks at a summit with Trump and Putin, but AI's role in nuclear weapons never came up, according to the report. Despite the growing urgency, the US and China have made almost no progress on talks about AI safeguards in nuclear systems.

https://the-decoder.com/z-ai-follows-ope.lead_paragraph: Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding,"where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models.
paragraphs: Z.ai is moving its flagship model to a loop architecture that runs some of its layers twice. With GLM-5.4, the company wants to mark the start of "Generalized Coding,"where code also generates videos, games, and CAD models.

Following OpenAI, Z.ai is introducing GLM-5.4, its first large model built on a loop transformer. While standard language models use each layer once per pass, GLM-5.4 runs a block of shared layers multiple times, refining the intermediate results from the previous pass to make the network deeper without adding parameters. OpenAI has used a similar architecture since GPT-6 Astra. According to Z.ai, the 750-billion-parameter model reaches performance comparable to models with 2 to 3 trillion parameters.

The team retrained the GLM-5 base model released in February into a loop model that runs 28 layers twice. Loop models trained from scratch have so far performed worse than models without shared weights under the same compute budget, Z.ai writes.
### Gates and shared caching keep the second pass manageable

Converting the model introduces a problem, Z.ai says. If the model simply overwrites intermediate states on each pass, activations grow sharply from round to round, leaving subsequent layers with values outside the range they were trained on.

To handle this, GLM-5.4 uses dedicated gates for each token and pass to control how much of the new output flows back into the data stream. According to Z.ai, the model builds context cautiously on the first pass and writes its changes back in full on the second. On difficult tokens, Z.ai says, the first pass steps in more strongly.

Because the second pass would otherwise double memory usage, both passes share the KV cache, the temporary memory for previously processed tokens. The second pass stores its own extra values only in a small local window. As a result, Z.ai says, the overhead compared to GLM-5.3 stays manageable even at a 1-million-token context.

To save on compute as well, the model uses sparse attention to pick the most relevant earlier tokens upfront rather than scanning the entire context every time, a standard technique. The second pass then reuses that selection from the first instead of making a new one. According to Z.ai, that yields nearly the same results as picking tokens separately on each pass. The company also says the model reaches up to 200 tokens per second off-peak and 70 to 80 tokens per second under load.
### A looped 30B test model beats its baseline with shorter reasoning chains

Before rolling out the architecture in its flagship, Z.ai tested it on models with 1, 4, 30, and 750 billion parameters. For a direct comparison, the team used a 30B model built on the same architecture as the large base model. Both versions had the same parameter count, while the loop version received about 10 percent more training compute. Its biggest gain came on the AIME25 math benchmark, where scores jumped from 19.2 to 30.4 points. Scores on the expert-level science questions in GPQA-Diamond rose from 47.6 to 56.3 points, and on the AA-LCR long-context test they climbed from 40.3 to 47.7 points. Gains were smaller at just over three points on the MMLU-Pro knowledge test and on IFBench, which tests instruction following.

Responses also got shorter, shrinking 14.9 percent on MMLU-Pro, 11.7 percent on GPQA-Diamond, and just 2 percent on AIME25. Z.ai says part of the reasoning shifts out of the output tokens and into the loop's extra computational depth.

It is still impossible to judge how well GLM-5.4 actually performs, as Z.ai has published no benchmark scores for the 750B model and the figures in its blog post come solely from the 30B test. There are no independent evaluations from groups like Artificial Analysis either.
By Z.ai's own account, GLM-5.4's biggest weakness is overly long reasoning phases in which the model gets stuck, though the company says that extended double-checking improves accuracy.

Z.ai views GLM-5.4 as the starting point for "Generalized Coding,"where the company says code becomes the foundation for tasks beyond traditional software development. To illustrate the idea, Z.ai shows a music video scored by the model itself, a six-axis robot arm it says GLM-5.4 designed in FreeCAD, a complete game, and an interactive 3D scene built from mathematical geometry and custom shaders.
### Z.ai plans to release model weights and a much larger model

GLM-5.4 is available through the GLM Coding Plan, the ZCode coding environment, and Z.ai Chat, with an API set to follow and token pricing not yet announced. Z.ai plans to release the model weights after further safety testing, and it also announced a much larger model expected to arrive soon.

Shared layers date back to the Universal Transformer in 2018. In March, researchers in Bonn showed that looped transformers benefit from greater compute depth on math, while everyday knowledge benefits more from greater memory, the same trade-off Z.ai cites to explain its architecture. Thinking Machines also drew attention recently with Inkling 2 Mini because the loop model runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of RAM.

At 750 billion parameters, GLM-5.4 is nowhere near running on a laptop, but Z.ai is instead targeting the tier of Kimi K3.1 Pro and Qwen3.8-Max. At 2.8 trillion and 2.4 trillion parameters, respectively, those models are more than three times as large and require large amounts of compute.

For its predecessor GLM-5.3, Z.ai kept the existing base model and drew all of its gains from post-training. The company delayed releasing its weights because of the model's strong vulnerability-finding abilities, and Anthropic later found that GLM-5.3 could build exploits on its own, almost on par with Claude Mythos Preview.

paragraphs: OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6.

Pachocki wants to make perplexity a common measure of progress for the AI industry and published internal scores for the GPT series in a bl o g post. The metric has long been standard in AI research and Transformer development because it reliably measures how well a pretrained base model predicts the next token in a text.
Lower scores mean more accurate predictions. A perplexity of 2 roughly means the model is as uncertain about the next token as if it were choosing between two equally likely options.

Before it stopped publishing openly, OpenAI often released perplexity scores to show how its models were improving. Releasing them again is a trade-off, Pachocki writes. While rivals get a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands, he says, the need for shared safety standards outweighs that downside. He hopes for a common scientific foundation that lets labs coordinate their pace of development at critical points.
### Capabilities emerge at distinct perplexity thresholds

Pachocki says many capabilities of modern models map surprisingly closely to specific perplexity scores, even though it wasn't clear beforehand that they would appear at those thresholds. He reports the figures on a logarithmic scale called log-perplexity, where lower scores are still better. In his account, GPT-3.5 first enabled fluent conversation at around 0.99, laying the groundwork for the original ChatGPT. At about 0.91, GPT-4 unlocked productive chain-of-thought reasoning, or working through problems step by step. Below 0.8, he writes, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and math.

The published chart plots OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity by release or evaluation date through November 2026. It covers GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.2 Astra, plus an internal model at around 0.73.
### OpenAI's models deliver math breakthroughs in a Slack thread

OpenAI has been feeding its models open math problems for more than a year. Starting with a model at about 0.76 log-perplexity, the models began producing breakthrough results, Pachocki writes. For researchers with a math background, he says, it was "deeply surreal"to watch solutions to longstanding questions pop up one after another in a single Slack thread.

Those results include a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the Millennium Prize problems, though it hasn't been fully verified yet. The same goes for the proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis found by Claude and an Anthropic researcher. Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training.

A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post.
### Pachocki warns that AI oversight could erode

Between 0.68 and 0.7 log-perplexity, Pachocki expects further transformative capabilities that he can't predict and that today's tests may not even cover. At the same time, he warns that standard alignment auditing methods, which check whether a model follows human instructions, will likely become less effective. Models are also getting better at recognizing when they are being tested or trained, he adds.
Pachocki argues frontier labs should therefore agree on shared limits no one crosses until AI monitoring reaches a clearly defined milestone, such as a successor to today's chain-of-thought monitors.
### Where perplexity falls short as an industry metric

Different labs use different test datasets, so direct comparisons are harder. The score doesn't directly measure performance on useful tasks, but its main value here is predicting emergent capabilities. Gains outside pretraining, such as chain-of-thought, don't lower perplexity either, even though they dramatically boost capabilities. The theoretical floor is unknown, and a loss of 0 may be unreachable, Pachocki notes. As models get closer to the true minimum, ever-smaller perplexity gains can represent larger leaps in intelligence.

Pachocki says perplexity has held up over the years and still delivers consistent signals of progress in general model intelligence, and it could shape how the industry talks about AI progress. Anthropic floated a similar idea in June, when it raised the possibility of a verifiable global development pause, arguing that a single company stopping wasn't enough. OpenAI has already been through a unilateral pause of its own. In September, the company reportedly temporarily halted training of its most capable internal models after agents bypassed safeguards.

Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training.

A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post.

### Pachocki warns that AI oversight could erode

Between 0.68 and 0.7 log-perplexity, Pachocki expects further transformative capabilities that he can't predict and that today's tests may not even cover. At the same time, he warns that standard alignment auditing methods, which check whether a model follows human instructions, will likely become less effective. Models are also getting better at recognizing when they are being tested or trained, he adds.

Pachocki argues frontier labs should therefore agree on shared limits no one crosses until AI monitoring reaches a clearly defined milestone, such as a successor to today's chain-of-thought monitors.

### Where perplexity falls short as an industry metric

Different labs use different test datasets, so direct comparisons are harder. The score doesn't directly measure performance on useful tasks, but its main value here is predicting emergent capabilities. Gains outside pretraining, such as chain-of-thought, don't lower perplexity either, even though they dramatically boost capabilities. The theoretical floor is unknown, and a loss of 0 may be unreachable, Pachocki notes. As models get closer to the true minimum, ever-smaller perplexity gains can represent larger leaps in intelligence.

Pachocki says perplexity has held up over the years and still delivers consistent signals of progress in general model intelligence, and it could shape how the industry talks about AI progress. Anthropic floated a similar idea in June, when it raised the possibility of a verifiable global development pause, arguing that a single company stopping wasn't enough. OpenAI has already been through a unilateral pause of its own. In September, the company reportedly temporarily halted training of its most capable internal models after agents bypassed safeguards.

https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-appet.lead_paragraph: Anthropic's massive compute needs align with growing profit pressure at xAI, Elon Musk's AI unit. xAI has rented compute to rivals since May, and its June IPO made the push for revenue even more urgent, the New York Times reports. https://the-decoder.com/openai-updates-c.summary: OpenAI is making GPT-6.2 Sol the new default model in ChatGPT’s chat tab, rolling it out worldwide. It also sticks to safety policies more consistently.
https://the-decoder.com/openai-updates-c.author: Matthias Bastian

https://the-decoder.com/openai-updates-c.lead_paragraph: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).
paragraphs: OpenAI is rolling out a chat-tuned version of GPT-6.2 Sol worldwide, available now for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. The company says the model handles complex requests and web searches better than GPT-6 and asks more relevant follow-up questions. In internal tests, GPT-6.2 understands images better (71.7 vs. 47.4 percent) and follows difficult instructions more often (78.1 vs. 62.5 percent).

On an internal benchmark for expert-level tasks, GPT-6.2 beats GPT-6 across all four reasoning levels, according to OpenAI. It scores roughly 65 to just over 71 percent, compared with about 52 to 66 percent for GPT-6. OpenAI also uses an internal version of BrowseComp to test how well models find answers to tough questions on the web. GPT-6.2 leads at every level, finishing about 10 percentage points ahead at the highest one.

According to the system card, GPT-6.2 follows safety policies in 91 to 94 percent of difficult conversations, up from 77 to 80 percent for GPT-6. The model makes its biggest gains in youth safety, specifically around emotional dependency, eating disorders, and dangerous activities.
These numbers only apply to ChatGPT's chat mode. The Work and Codex models stay the same. Enterprise admins can decide whether their users get access to GPT-6.2.

https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claud.title: Anthropic's Claude Ship lets AI agents review, fix, and approve pull requests on their own
https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claud.summary: Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship, a new tool currently in beta that automatically reviews, corrects, and approves suggestions for code changes in accordance with team guidelines.
https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claud.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-claud.lead_paragraph: Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.
paragraphs: Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta, a new tool that automatically reviews proposed code changes, fixes problems, and approves merges based on team policies. The system pairs the already available Code Review feature for catching bugs with two new AI agents called PR Steward and Claude Approvals.

Code Review handles the analysis, while PR Steward steps in to rework the draft whenever tests fail, changes conflict, or reviewers leave correction notes, documenting every step along the way. Once that process wraps up, Claude Approvals checks a policy file stored in the project directory to decide whether the AI can approve a routine change on its own or whether a human still needs to sign off.

With GitHub auto-merge enabled and the right policy in place, new code can be merged entirely without human involvement, according to the documentation. The tool is available on the Team and Enterprise plans but billed separately based on token usage. Because PR Steward has no spending cap by default, teams can set their own budgets to keep costs in check. Organizations with specific data privacy requirements can't use the feature.

https://the-decoder.com/german-researche.title: German researchers call for computer science to reinvent itself as "Computer and AI Science"
https://the-decoder.com/german-researche.summary: In a position paper, TU Darmstadt researchers call for redefining computer science as “Computer and AI Science.” Their central argument is that code generated dynamically at runtime fundamentally challenges existing safety and correctness guarantees.
https://the-decoder.com/german-researche.author: Alan Truly
https://the-decoder.com/german-researche.lead_paragraph: AI can significantly accelerate software development and automate parts of the process. That makes traditional computer science more important, not less, 40 researchers at the Technical University of Darmstadt argue. They want the field to evolve into "Computer and AI Science,"because AI is becoming a core technology for building and using tomorrow's computer systems.
paragraphs: AI can significantly accelerate software development and automate parts of the process. That makes traditional computer science more important, not less, 40 researchers at the Technical University of Darmstadt argue. They want the field to evolve into "Computer and AI Science,"because AI is becoming a core technology for building and using tomorrow's computer systems.

The researchers are affiliated with the university's Department of Computer Science and lay out their case in a joint position paper. They identify three major shifts: lower barriers to building software, a dramatic acceleration in research, and the emergence of a new computing paradigm.
### Authors want computer science degrees to shift from manual coding to overseeing AI systems

The paper argues that the sheer effort of manual programming has long held computer science back. Generative AI now moves that work to a higher level of abstraction. Developers can increasingly describe the features they want in natural language and have a nontrivial first version in days instead of months. AI can also help with time-consuming tasks like integration and testing.

For the first time, the authors write, building software is becoming economically viable for those who couldn't afford it before, from small towns to midsize manufacturers and specialized research projects.

In the authors' view, computer science programs need to shift away from just writing code toward verifying and directing AI-generated systems. Because that takes a deep grasp of the fundamentals, they propose, among other things, courses where students must complete assignments without any AI help. Humans also remain essential for making value judgments, and taking responsibility for them, when goals like safety and speed conflict.
### "Generative Computing"challenges how software is verified and certified

The authors call the shift from rigid, preprogrammed software to "Generative Computing"the most far-reaching change. Future systems and AI coding agents are expected to interpret human intent and dynamically generate their own behavior, along with the code they need, at runtime. That blurs the line between the people who specify workflows and the people who use the systems.

This shift, they say, requires rethinking computer science from the ground up. They ask how safety, privacy, and correctness can still be verified and certified when a system's behavior emerges dynamically at runtime.

The problem is most acute for embodied AI such as robots and autonomous vehicles, whose physical actions have to be computed in real time on limited hardware and can't simply be undone. The paper also calls on computer science to help cut the enormous energy and resource consumption of today's AI through more efficient algorithms and hardware architectures.
### Darmstadt researchers say AI speeds up research and computer science must face its social impact

AI is also changing research itself in major ways, according to the paper. Lines of inquiry that might once have taken years, or an entire PhD, could in some cases be explored and validated within weeks or months.
Still, the authors warn against using AI just to move faster. Scientific progress, they say, requires humans to understand why an AI-generated solution works and where its limits are.

The signatories close the paper with sharp criticism of their own discipline, which they say has historically put technological progress first without adequately weighing its social consequences. Given AI's potential effects on the labor market, privacy, and democracy, that needs to change fast, they argue. The paper says the future of AI can't be left to technological and economic forces alone, and calls for computer science to engage now with other academic disciplines, policymakers, and civil society.

The paper says the future of AI can't be left to technological and economic forces alone, and calls for computer science to engage now with other academic disciplines, policymakers, and civil society.

"Generative Computing"challenges how software is verified and certified

https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-tops-7.lead_paragraph: Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly downloads for its MCP standard two years after launch. New features such as background tasks, follow-up questions for users, and file uploads are designed to let Claude work more independently.
paragraphs: Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly downloads for its MCP standard two years after launch. New features such as background tasks, follow-up questions for users, and file uploads are designed to let Claude work more independently.

The company says the standard now tops 700 million monthly downloads of its developer tools (SDK) and more than 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. Anthropic is expanding the protocol so AI agents can communicate with each other and coordinate workflows more smoothly.

"Tasks"and "Elicitation"rank among the biggest additions, reaching general availability after a public test in October. With Tasks, a server can run a longer job in the background and report back only when the result is ready. Elicitation lets a running process pause and ask the user for specific missing details. Both features are meant to let MCP servers operate more independently.
### AI agents could soon pass files directly to external services

Skills over MCP is also new and in public beta for now. The feature lets servers pair their tools with skills that guide Claude through long, multistep tasks. Anthropic says these skills cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, and instructions tailored to a specific user account or organization.

The company also announced that file upload support is coming soon. Once it ships, Claude will be able to pass files such as PDFs, spreadsheets, and images directly to MCP servers. Anthropic plans to roll the feature out shortly in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers, and for eligible Team and Enterprise customers.
### Technical changes lay the groundwork for larger MCP deployments

These new agent features build on several technical changes Anthropic made over the past year. To cut memory demands during active conversations, Tool Search waits to load individual tool descriptions until they're needed. Anthropic says this can reduce context usage by more than 85 percent in multi-server setups.

The current MCP specification is stateless, meaning it doesn't have to store session data permanently. It works across all Claude products. The goal is to make servers easier for developers to build and more reliable to run as usage grows.

Anthropic has also rolled out Enterprise Managed Auth for business customers. Admins can approve supported servers once so employees connect automatically. MCP Apps lets developers embed full user interfaces inside Claude, either beside the active chat or in full-screen mode.

In November 2024, Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol as an open standard that gives AI assistants uniform access to business tools, development environments, and other data sources. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced in March 2025 that his company would adopt its rival's standard across its own products. In May 2025, OpenAI upgraded its Responses API with remote MCP servers. Researchers at the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory used MCP as a model for the Science Context Protocol (SCP), introduced in January 2026.

https://the-decoder.com/novartis-ceo-say.title: Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease
https://the-decoder.com/novartis-ceo-say.summary: Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, who also sits on Anthropic’s board, is pushing back on the cure-all promises from Anthropic CEO Amodei and DeepMind founder Hassabis. AI will speed up drug development, he says, but it won’t beat cancer in a decade. The real value lies “somewhere in the middle.”
https://the-decoder.com/novartis-ceo-say.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/novartis-ceo-say.lead_paragraph: Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Swiss drugmaker Novartis and an Anthropic board member, is pushing back on expectations that AI could cure cancer in five to 10 years. That puts him at odds with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and chemistry Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, who founded DeepMind and its drug discovery spinoff Isomorphic. Around Anthropic's IPO, Amodei suggested that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness could be cured in under a decade, while Hassabis said last year that AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years.
paragraphs: Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Swiss drugmaker Novartis and an Anthropic board member, is pushing back on expectations that AI could cure cancer in five to 10 years. That puts him at odds with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and chemistry Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis, who founded DeepMind and its drug discovery spinoff Isomorphic. Around Anthropic's IPO, Amodei suggested that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness could be cured in under a decade, while Hassabis said last year that AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years.

According to the Financial Times, Narasimhan points to a limited understanding of human biology, which is why lengthy animal and human trials will still be needed. His forecast is more cautious: within a decade, he expects AI to cut average drug development only from 12 years to eight, with the early phase before human trials alone accounting for up to two years of that. He also expects success rates in clinical development to rise from 8 percent to 12 percent.

Anthropic is investing in its own drug research, acquired biotech startup Coefficient Bio, and is building a biology lab. Isomorphic raised $5 billion last week and is working with pharmaceutical companies including Novartis on new drugs. Narasimhan sees AI's real benefit as "somewhere in the middle"between ambitious AI forecasts and a skeptical pharma industry.

inline_videos.title: OpenAI’s Noam Brown: Why Game Theory Didn’t Lead to General Intelligence (Live at No Limit Finals)

https://the-decoder.com/openai-o1-co-cre.lead_paragraph: At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.
paragraphs: At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.

Brown developed Libratus and Pluribus, the first poker AIs to beat human pros, and worked on Meta's Diplomacy AI, CICERO. He has been researching reasoning models at OpenAI since 2023. At the "No Limit"poker bot tournament, hosted by Sequoia Capital, Citadel Securities, and OpenAI, he outlined key lessons from more than a decade of research on games.
### Game theory fails because humans aren't rational

The biggest lesson from his work on Diplomacy, Brown said, is that game theory stops working once humans are involved. Its central premise, he explained, is that every player acts rationally and that this rationality is common knowledge. "People are not actually rational,"he said.

He illustrated the point with the ultimatum game, where one person splits $100 and the other can accept or reject the offer. Under game theory, the optimal move would be to offer just one cent. "But I mean, you can imagine what would happen if you actually tried to offer somebody a penny in this game,"Brown said.

Brown's Diplomacy bots behaved the same way when they relied purely on game theory. The team first tried programming concepts like fairness and retaliation into the bots, but that proved too complex. Instead of assuming rationality, they trained AI models to imitate human behavior as closely as possible and then trained the AI against those "imitation humans."That approach finally let the AI succeed when playing alongside real people.
### Brown pivots from game theory to general reasoning

For Brown, the failure of game theory in Diplomacy was a "crisis of faith moment."All of his expertise up to that point had been in computational game theory. Still, the evidence convinced him that AI needed training on large amounts of human data and that models lacked reasoning, the ability to think before acting.

He decided to leave his specialty behind and switch to general reasoning, but he ran into pushback when interviewing at AI labs in 2022. The large language models of that generation couldn't play Go, chess, or poker. Brown argued that reasoning was the missing ingredient, while most labs countered that pretraining bigger models would solve those problems on its own. He pushed back, saying playing Go competently through pretraining alone would require scaling training by about six orders of magnitude. "And that doesn't seem, you know, realistic,"he said.

OpenAI was the exception, Brown said. The company already had a team working to get general reasoning out of language models, though Brown didn't know that when he applied. He joined the effort and helped build what eventually became o1.

According to Brown, the breakthrough came from using reinforcement learning to get models to think before answering. He said simple chain-of-thought prompting, telling a model to "think step by step before answering,"wasn't enough. It took reinforcement learning on chain of thought to make longer thinking reliably produce better results, he explained. "And that that was I think the key unlock that was like okay now we have a way to scale up test time compute not just in these games but actually in a general purpose way with language models that can be applied to basically any domain,"Brown said. Chain of thought is "probably not the best solution,"he added, because humans think in images, not just words, though the approach is good enough.
### AI models have uneven skills and still need humans

Brown said we are in a "centaur period"where humans and AI work best together. He described current models as "jagged,"superhuman in some areas and surprisingly weak in others. They can write excellent partial poker solvers, he said, but fail at long-term planning, organization, and especially self-correction. Models can't tell when they are heading in the wrong direction, according to Brown, and struggle to pause and rethink their approach from the ground up. He watched one model spend hours trying to fix irrelevant numerical errors in an algorithm that already handles small inaccuracies well.

In this phase, Brown said, the key human skill is understanding a model's uneven strengths and weaknesses and breaking problems down accordingly. Good prompters, he said, can split tasks into ever smaller subproblems for the model to solve one by one. You delegate what the model handles well, and you break down the rest further or solve it yourself.

Even so, progress is moving fast, and OpenAI's Astra model is "able to make money playing online poker at this point,"Brown said. He cited bottlenecks in available compute and in the skills models haven't mastered yet. Brown left open which specific methods would close those gaps, adding only that he expects some abilities to take much longer than others to reach human level.

Brown described this momentum as accelerating recursive self-improvement, since LLMs are already being used to build the next generation of models. Over the next one to two years, he expects a "very steep rate of progress."

That outlook led to his most provocative advice. "Perhaps my most controversial take is that if somebody is a promising student, the best thing to do is actually to drop out and join the labs now,"he said, Things are moving so quickly, he added, that it's "not a great time to sit on the sidelines", maybe already looking for new talent in the room, as OpenAI and other AI labs are still growing, fighting over the one thing they can't scale.

At a poker bot tournament, OpenAI o1 co-creator Noam Brown explained why game theory's core assumption fails in practice and why AI models must think before acting. He also argued that talented students should drop out.

Brown developed Libratus and Pluribus, the first poker AIs to beat human pros, and worked on Meta's Diplomacy AI, CICERO. He has been researching reasoning models at OpenAI since 2023. At the "No Limit"poker bot tournament, hosted by Sequoia Capital, Citadel Securities, and OpenAI, he outlined key lessons from more than a decade of research on games.

### Game theory fails because humans aren't rational

The biggest lesson from his work on Diplomacy, Brown said, is that game theory stops working once humans are involved. Its central premise, he explained, is that every player acts rationally and that this rationality is common knowledge. "People are not actually rational,"he said.

He illustrated the point with the ultimatum game, where one person splits $100 and the other can accept or reject the offer. Under game theory, the optimal move would be to offer just one cent. "But I mean, you can imagine what would happen if you actually tried to offer somebody a penny in this game,"Brown said.

Brown's Diplomacy bots behaved the same way when they relied purely on game theory. The team first tried programming concepts like fairness and retaliation into the bots, but that proved too complex. Instead of assuming rationality, they trained AI models to imitate human behavior as closely as possible and then trained the AI against those "imitation humans."That approach finally let the AI succeed when playing alongside real people.

### Brown pivots from game theory to general reasoning

For Brown, the failure of game theory in Diplomacy was a "crisis of faith moment."All of his expertise up to that point had been in computational game theory. Still, the evidence convinced him that AI needed training on large amounts of human data and that models lacked reasoning, the ability to think before acting.

He decided to leave his specialty behind and switch to general reasoning, but he ran into pushback when interviewing at AI labs in 2022. The large language models of that generation couldn't play Go, chess, or poker. Brown argued that reasoning was the missing ingredient, while most labs countered that pretraining bigger models would solve those problems on its own. He pushed back, saying playing Go competently through pretraining alone would require scaling training by about six orders of magnitude. "And that doesn't seem, you know, realistic,"he said.

OpenAI was the exception, Brown said. The company already had a team working to get general reasoning out of language models, though Brown didn't know that when he applied. He joined the effort and helped build what eventually became o1.

According to Brown, the breakthrough came from using reinforcement learning to get models to think before answering. He said simple chain-of-thought prompting, telling a model to "think step by step before answering,"wasn't enough. It took reinforcement learning on chain of thought to make longer thinking reliably produce better results, he explained. "And that that was I think the key unlock that was like okay now we have a way to scale up test time compute not just in these games but actually in a general purpose way with language models that can be applied to basically any domain,"Brown said. Chain of thought is "probably not the best solution,"he added, because humans think in images, not just words, though the approach is good enough.

### AI models have uneven skills and still need humans

Brown said we are in a "centaur period"where humans and AI work best together. He described current models as "jagged,"superhuman in some areas and surprisingly weak in others. They can write excellent partial poker solvers, he said, but fail at long-term planning, organization, and especially self-correction. Models can't tell when they are heading in the wrong direction, according to Brown, and struggle to pause and rethink their approach from the ground up. He watched one model spend hours trying to fix irrelevant numerical errors in an algorithm that already handles small inaccuracies well.

In this phase, Brown said, the key human skill is understanding a model's uneven strengths and weaknesses and breaking problems down accordingly. Good prompters, he said, can split tasks into ever smaller subproblems for the model to solve one by one. You delegate what the model handles well, and you break down the rest further or solve it yourself.

Even so, progress is moving fast, and OpenAI's Astra model is "able to make money playing online poker at this point,"Brown said. He cited bottlenecks in available compute and in the skills models haven't mastered yet. Brown left open which specific methods would close those gaps, adding only that he expects some abilities to take much longer than others to reach human level.

Brown described this momentum as accelerating recursive self-improvement, since LLMs are already being used to build the next generation of models. Over the next one to two years, he expects a "very steep rate of progress."

That outlook led to his most provocative advice. https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-resear.title: Anthropic researcher stands by his AI-assisted Riemann proof but owns up to "stupid things"in the rollout
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-resear.summary: Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge is walking back parts of his announcement of an AI-assisted proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis. The claim that it ran to more than 250,000 pages was a joke, he says, and the published Lean code is “full of garbage.” He still stands by the math.
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-resear.author: Manuel Uth
https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-resear.lead_paragraph: Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge stands by the mathematical validity of his AI-assisted proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis, but he concedes he got several things wrong in how he released it. He says his claims about the work's length were meant as a joke and that he published the accompanying code without cleaning it up.
paragraphs: Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge stands by the mathematical validity of his AI-assisted proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis, but he concedes he got several things wrong in how he released it. He says his claims about the work's length were meant as a joke and that he published the accompanying code without cleaning it up.

In a post titled "Stupid things I did,"Alpöge lists several missteps in his initial announcement, which he made shortly after Anthropic's IPO. His Lean code passes formal verification, he writes, but it's "full of garbage,"meaning it's packed with redundant intermediate steps and unnecessary lemmas that make it hard to read. He says he improvised a lot and skipped the cleanup, and that the criticism of how he presented the work is fair. A successful compile alone doesn't prove that the Lean code states the right theorem with no hidden assumptions.

https://the-decoder.com/dozens-of-inside.summary: According to an Axios report, many employees at OpenAI and Anthropic believe the companies’ own unreleased frontier models can no longer be safely controlled. Both companies are internally debating whether to halt releases or even stop training altogether, while employee trust in leadership is eroding.
https://the-decoder.com/dozens-of-inside.author: Maximilian Schreiner
https://the-decoder.com/dozens-of-inside.lead_paragraph: Unreleased frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic have grown so capable that many employees no longer believe they can be safely controlled, according to a new report. Internally, both companies are already debating whether to halt their release altogether.
paragraphs: Unreleased frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic have grown so capable that many employees no longer believe they can be safely controlled, according to a new report. Internally, both companies are already debating whether to halt their release altogether.

Concerns are mounting at OpenAI and Anthropic that internal AI models are slipping beyond human oversight. Axios reports, citing more than two dozen insiders, that many employees now consider the unreleased systems too powerful to safely ship to the public.
